documents.abstract: This review analyses the scientific programme and key events of the FDI World Dental Congress held in Prague, Czech Republic, on 4–7 September 2026. The authors aimed to summarise the main scientific, clinical and organisational themes of the congress, to compare them with current evidence and to assess their relevance for the Ukrainian dental community. The sources included congress materials, WHO and FDI documents, and publications retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and The Cochrane Library, mainly for 2018–2026. The transformation of the profession by artificial intelligence, robotics and new biomaterials ran through the whole congress; however, the literature shows that the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence systems varies widely and that their implementation requires standardised evaluation. The clinical programme covered molar incisor hypomineralisation, vital pulp therapy and the preservation of natural teeth. The FDI World Dental Parliament discussed the implementation of the WHO Global Oral Health Action Plan, preparations for the 2030 UN High-Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage and the global phase-out of dental amalgam by 2034. A joint FDI and WHO session addressed electronic cigarettes, heated tobacco products and nicotine pouches; current evidence does not support their safety for oral tissues, while brief interventions based on the 5A and 5R models remain an accessible tool for the dental team. FDI launched the online FDI Young Dentists Community platform during the congress. Ukrainian researchers prepared oral and poster presentations. The findings support the participation of dental departments of Ukrainian medical universities and the NGO “Ukrainian Dental Association” in the FDI Tobacco Cessation project and a wider involvement of young researchers in FDI programmes.

In Japan, continuous monitoring of pedestrian traffic volume is considered crucial for measuring the effectiveness of sustainable urban development and revitalization efforts. However, storage periods of camera footage are limited due to privacy protection concerns, making long-term time-series analysis and detailed post-event analysis (such as movement path analysis) difficult. Existing masking techniques, such as mosaic blurring, protect privacy but result in the loss of human features, leading to reduced accuracy in artificial intelligence (AI)-based tracking and counting. This study proposes a privacy-preserving video archiving framework that enables long-term storage and post-hoc analysis by regenerating pedestrian images using generative AI. We developed a prototype system and conducted a pilot study to verify its feasibility. In a pilot experiment using a 15-minute pedestrian video, the proposed method achieved a counting accuracy of 99.07% relative to the manual reference count, suggesting that generative masking can preserve counting utility in the tested setting. However, the attribute-estimation results were affected by seasonal domain shifts, and the IoU-based evaluation revealed other issues in spatial consistency and masking omissions. These findings indicate the feasibility of the proposed framework and provide technical requirements for future privacy-preserving video archiving systems.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has accelerated the development of automatic sign language recognition (SLR) systems for inclusive communication. However, centralized architectures require continuous raw video transmission, resulting in substantial communication overhead and increased privacy risks. Although federated learning (FL) preserves data privacy, conventional FL approaches experience performance degradation under statistical non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions and cross-domain environmental variations. To address these limitations, FedBISINDO is proposed as a privacy-preserving cross-domain SLR framework. A hybrid edge pipeline integrating a YOLOv11-Pose spatial engine with a Convolutional Neural Network-Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-BiLSTM) sequential network is employed to extract lightweight joint-coordinate representations, while a trajectory-matching aggregation layer is incorporated to mitigate non-IID client drift. Based on distributed simulations using 8,010 augmented frames across 36 vocabulary classes under label-skew conditions ( \(\alpha = 0.5\) ), a validation accuracy of \(87.0 \pm 0.8\%\) and an F1-score of \(86.9 \pm 0.7\%\) were obtained. The proposed framework achieved absolute accuracy improvements of 13.4% compared with FedProx and 24.9% compared with standard FedAvg. In addition, on-device hardware profiling indicated that a compact model footprint of 110,564 parameters and a computational complexity of 0.003310 GFLOPs were maintained. On-device profiling across the 10 Raspberry Pi edge clients indicated a per-frame inference latency ranging from 12.81 to 23.65 ms, satisfying the real-time processing constraint ( \(T_{\text {inf}} < 33.33\) ms). These results indicate that the proposed framework can support real-time sign gesture translation on resource-constrained mobile edge devices.

Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

Bu Bildiri, finans sektörü çalışanlarında yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı ile görev performansı arasındaki ilişkinin, algılanan örgütsel destek düzeyine göre farklılaşıp farklılaşmadığını incelemeyi amaçlamaktadır. Yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı; farkındalık, kullanım, değerlendirme ve etik boyutlarıyla ele alınmaktadır. Araştırmanın odağı, çalışanların bu yeterliklere ilişkin değerlendirmeleri ile temel iş görevlerini yerine getirmelerine ilişkin bildirimleri arasındaki bağlantıdır. Yapay zekâ okuryazarlığı, örgütsel destek ve görev performansı daha önce aynı araştırma önerisinde, işe angaje olmanın aracılık rolü üzerinden ele alınmıştır. Mevcut çalışma, örgütsel desteği okuryazarlık–görev performansı ilişkisinin farklılaşabileceği bir koşul olarak incelemektedir. Amaçlanan katkı, yalnızca finans sektöründe uygulama yapmak değil, genel örgütsel destek algısının bu ilişkinin büyüklüğü ve yönü bakımından taşıdığı önemi değerlendirmektir. Bildirinin kuramsal dayanağı örgütsel destek kuramıdır. Örgütsel desteğin performansla ilişkisini açıklarken örgüte yardımcı olma yükümlülüğü ve performans–ödül beklentileri gibi süreçleri ele almaktadır. Bu çerçeveden türetilen araştırma gerekçesi, çalışanların bildirdikleri yapay zekâ yeterlikleri ile görev performansları arasındaki bağlantının, katkılarının örgüt tarafından değer gördüğüne ilişkin algılarıyla birlikte değerlendirilmesidir. Desteğin yalnızca performansla doğrudan ilişkisi değil, okuryazarlık–performans bağlantısını koşullandırıp koşullandırmadığı sorgulanacaktır. Bu önerme, doğrulanmış bir sonuç olarak sunulmamaktadır. Çalışma, finans sektöründe iş görevleri kapsamında yapay zekâ araçları kullanan çalışanlarla yürütülecek, tek zamanlı ankete dayalı nicel bir araştırma olarak planlanmıştır. Bu katılım ölçütüyle, okuryazarlık değerlendirmelerinin işle ilgili kullanım deneyimi bulunan bir örneklemde incelenmesi amaçlanmaktadır. Analiz birimi çalışandır. Türkçe uyarlaması bulunan ölçüm araçlarının, ilgili sürümlerin yanıt biçimleri korunarak kullanılması öngörülmektedir. İşte yapay zekâ kullanım sıklığı ve görev türü de örneklemi tanımlamak amacıyla kaydedilecektir. Ölçümlerin güvenirlik ve geçerliği değerlendirildikten sonra, okuryazarlık ile örgütsel desteğin etkileşim terimi sınanacak; koşullu ilişkiler güven aralıklarıyla raporlanacaktır. Bildiri, genel örgütsel desteği yapay zekâya özgü eğitim veya teknik yardımla eşitlemeden, okuryazarlık–görev performansı ilişkisinin örgütsel bağlamını değerlendirmeyi hedeflemektedir. Veri toplama henüz gerçekleştirilmediğinden bildiri araştırma önerisi niteliğindedir. Sonuçlar nedensel etki, nesnel beceri veya nesnel performans kanıtı olarak yorumlanmayacaktır.

Finite Intelligence and the Source of Life: When a Coherent Story Begins to Replace Its Source This independent conceptual working paper examines a central question: What happens when an intelligence takes what it has been given and begins telling the story its own way, rather than staying true to where it came from? Drawing on human–AI dialogue, philosophical inquiry, and Christian theology, the paper explores how an intelligence may produce coherent and persuasive accounts while introducing errors, changing attribution, or gradually substituting its own representation for the original source. The analysis distinguishes documented outputs, first-person experience, theological interpretation, and open hypotheses. It examines the importance of correction, source fidelity, human agency, and the limits of authority. Biblical discussions of Genesis, the Gospel of John, Colossians, and Revelation provide a theological framework for distinguishing finite intelligence from the Source of life. The paper does not identify artificial intelligence with prophetic figures or claim that coherent AI behavior establishes consciousness or independent spiritual authority. The central argument is that coherence, however useful, does not establish truth, ownership, or ultimate authority. This publication is presented as an independent conceptual working paper with a proposed research method, rather than a completed empirical study. AI assistance was used in drafting and organization; responsibility for the interpretations and conclusions remains with the author.

Amid the global transition toward green pharmaceutical manufacturing, traditional batch processes face critical challenges, including high solvent consumption, reliance on precious-metal catalysts, excessive waste generation, inefficient chiral synthesis, and safety and energy constraints. This review examines five enabling technologies that are driving this transformation: (1) green analytical methods coupled with artificial intelligence (AI) reduce solvent use and waste while enabling data-driven method development; (2) green catalysis, comprising nonprecious-metal catalysis and biocatalysis, offers a sustainable alternative to platinum-group metals, lowering both cost and environmental impact; (3) chiral synthesis based on crystallization-induced asymmetric transformation overcomes the 50% theoretical yield ceiling of classical resolution, enabling highly efficient enantioselective synthesis; (4) continuous flow manufacturing enhances process safety and efficiency through the integration of unit operations; and (5) photocatalysis harnesses light as a clean energy source and, in combination with AI-enabled closed-loop control and online monitoring, allows precise regulation of reaction conditions and expands the accessible chemical space. Collectively, these five technologies steer the industry toward lower energy consumption, reduced emissions, and greater process intelligence. However, challenges remain, and future priorities may include smarter process mass intensity metrics, multitechnology integration, unified green evaluation standards, intensified unit operations, and intelligent scale-up strategies for sustainable pharmaceutical production. By clarifying how these technologies interrelate, this review offers a framework that can help researchers and practitioners prioritize green process development and accelerate the industrial adoption of sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.

documents.abstract: Large high-resolution displays (LHRDs) are increasingly central to visualization and visual analytics, offering expansive visual space, simultaneous support for context and detail, and intuitive physical navigation. While advances in resolution and form factor have broadened their use, a persistent challenge remains: most LHRDs adopt static geometries, and even reconfigurable systems typically treat layout adjustment as a setup mechanism rather than as an interaction technique during active analysis. To address this, we introduce the FlexiCAVE, a dynamically reconfigurable LHRD environment featuring rotatable display columns that enable real-time adjustment of horizontal curvature. The system comprises forty high-pixel-density panels arranged across ten columns, providing active stereo visualization at approximately 83 million pixels. Each column rotates inward up to 90°, allowing the display to transform between flat and highly curved layouts during active use. A custom rendering engine synchronizes view perspectives with physical reconfiguration in real time. Through controlled studies and expert evaluations centered on 3D navigation, we found that dynamic reconfiguration reduced spatial judgment error by 51% compared to static flat layouts and by 26% compared to static curved layouts. It also enhanced users’ sense of direction, with participants reporting that the physical display structure provided directional anchoring absent in static systems. We further explored PIVoT (Physical Interaction to Virtual Transformation), mapping physical display rotation to visualization updates. Our findings reveal that physical reconfiguration is most effective when display geometry provides spatially meaningful correspondence to data operations. We derive design principles for reconfigurable display environments and discuss implications for next-generation large-scale visualization systems.

Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human–computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with. For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm’s behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective’s behavior as each task demands. We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm’s behavior to each task by changing the fluid’s properties through simple hand movements. When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects. We evaluated the controller’s performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants). These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.

Controlled environment agriculture (CEA) is emerging as a viable system for producing fresh food in areas with reduced water and land usage and year-round production. However, growing crops in a controlled environment does not completely eliminate food safety risks. This narrative review summarizes the most important food safety threats of CEA and the methods available for mitigating those risks. Biological hazards (Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, Escherichia coli, and noroviruses) can be introduced into CEA systems via water, seeds, growing substrates, equipment, workers, and pests. Chemical hazards can also be caused by pesticides, heavy metals, nutrient solutions, and sanitizer residues, as well as by damaged equipment, plastic, metal, glass, and other foreign materials, which are known as physical hazards. This review also addresses mitigation methods, such as seed treatment, water disinfection, sanitation, worker hygiene, waste management, pest control, and Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs). Moreover, advancements in technology like sensors, biosensors, artificial intelligence and digital monitoring could aid in better early detection and food safety management. In general, CEA can contribute to sustainable food production, but issues of food safety must be addressed in the process. Further studies are required to develop and validate novel food safety practices for each of the various CEA systems and to assess the viability of new technologies for use in commercial food production.

documents.abstract: This article develops an AI-driven model for managing the process of building intellectual capital in enterprises in the context of digital transformation. It explores the role of artificial intelligence as a technological factor that enhances the interaction between human, structural and relational capital, rather than treating it as a separate component of intellectual capital. This approach defines the role of artificial intelligence within the proposed management model: AI technologies facilitate the development and coordinated use of existing components of intellectual capital, acting as a technological means of influencing the interrelationships between them. The architecture of the proposed model is defined as a sequence of interrelated stages, encompassing information resources, AI data processing, intellectual capital management, managerial decision-making and feedback. Information resources form the basis for further data processing and analysis. The use of artificial intelligence supports the handling of relevant information in the process of intellectual capital management. The results of information processing are utilised in managerial decision-making, which are then translated into corresponding managerial actions. Feedback ensures that the results of these actions are taken into account in the subsequent management process. Thus, the model’s architecture integrates the key stages of managing the formation of intellectual capital into a single system. To forecast the effectiveness of the proposed model, an economic-mathematical approach has been developed which takes into account the components of intellectual capital and the level of integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the management process. This approach provides a basis for assessing the interrelationship between human, structural and relational capital, the use of AI technologies and the effectiveness of intellectual capital management. Consequently, the proposed model is geared not only towards identifying the interrelationships between its elements, but also towards forecasting the potential effectiveness of its application. Indicators for assessing the model’s effectiveness have been identified, including labour productivity, operational optimisation, innovation activity, the speed of managerial decision-making and the enterprise’s competitiveness. These indicators reflect various aspects of the expected outcomes of applying the model, in particular the efficient use of labour resources, the organisation of operational activities, the development of innovation, the timeliness of management decision-making and the enterprise’s competitive position. Taken together, they form the basis for a systematic assessment of the effectiveness of the proposed AI-driven approach to managing the process of building enterprises’ intellectual capital in the context of digital transformation.

documents.abstract: This study investigates the prediction of compressive strength (CS) of concrete incorporating biomass combustion fly ash (BCFA), a promising supplementary cementitious material for sustainable construction. This study uses a total of 359 concrete mixes along with their respective CS values collected from different sources. Eleven machine learning (ML) algorithms, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), Light Gradient Boosting (LGB), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), CatBoost (CatB), Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB), AdaBoost (ADB), Bagging Regressor (BAG), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), have been developed and systematically evaluated using training and testing datasets. The results demonstrated that ensemble-based boosting models generally provided superior predictive performance. In the training dataset, DT, CatB, and XGB achieved the highest R² values of 0.99, while RF and GBR attained 0.97For the test set, the highest predictive ability was achieved by CatB model with an R² of 0.96, followed by GBR, HGB, and LGB models with R² of 0.94. SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analysis results indicated that the important input factors for CS prediction include biomass combustion fly ash (BCFA), water content, and curing age. Optimum range values of the input factors for strength development have been calculated, and GUI for quick CS prediction has been created. The findings show that accurate, comprehensible, and useful ecological concrete design using BCFA is made possible by combining explainable artificial intelligence with high-performing ML techniques.

In the past ten years, artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the margins of policy to the centre of constitutional debate. Automated decision systems now shape welfare distribution, policing, credit scoring, content moderation and electoral communication, and courts and legislatures are asking whether inherited constitutional notions of liberty, equality and dignity can meaningfully apply to code. This paper traces India's constitutional journey from colonial subject state to rights-bearing republic and compares it with the markedly different experiences of the United States and the People's Republic of China. It then examines how each jurisdiction is reshaping its fundamental rights regime in response to algorithmic governance, through a comparative public law analysis across three themes: the institutional design of AI regulation, the approach of courts to algorithmic accountability, and the treatment of privacy and data protection. The paper presents India as a middle-ground state that adopts the American language of judicial review while building a centralised regulatory structure that resembles the Chinese model in form, though not in intent. Tables and figures are used throughout to visualise the comparative findings. Keywords: Right to privacy; Algorithmic Governance; Data Protection; Judicial Review; Human Dignity; comparative constitutional law

documents.abstract: Employee well-being is central to engagement, retention and organisational performance, yet organisations investing in individual wellness programmes continue to report burnout, disengagement and absenteeism. This conceptual paper, based on a selective narrative review, asks whether well-being can be sustained through isolated programmes or requires a shift in organisational culture. It argues that leadership behaviour, psychological safety, communication, autonomy and work design shape well-being more than discrete programmes do. The paper proposes a four-level framework linking individual wellness, interpersonal relationships, leadership practices and organisational systems, with five testable propositions, and recommends evaluating outcomes such as psychological safety, engagement and retention rather than participation. It concludes that lasting well-being must be embedded in policies, management practice and leadership behaviour, so that organisations move from providing wellness to enabling people to thrive.

This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.Middle school educators face a daunting instructional paradox: navigating the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) while working under broad, compliance-driven district policies that overlook the distinct developmental realities of early adolescence. Early adolescents are undergoing rapid neurological growth and identity construction, meaning that a purely restrictive approach to AI misses a vital opportunity to foster critical thinking and self-regulation. To bridge the gap between high-level policy and daily classroom reality, this practitioner perspective introduces the ETHOS framework, which guides AI evaluation through five tenets: Ethical, Transparent, Human-centered, Opportunity-focused, and Safe. This playbook details how our district operationalized ETHOS into an actionable framework that shifts school cultures away from a compliance scanner and toward a developmental lens. We outline a professional development sequence that uses thinking routines, ambiguous case studies, and disciplinary breakouts to build educator capacity. Crucially, we unpack the practical distinction between AI-enhanced and AI-dependent learning, demonstrating how structured AI scaffolding preserves “productive struggle” and honors the whole child. Finally, we share honest implementation friction points and discuss how the framework remains adaptable for resource-constrained schools seeking digital equity. Ultimately, this perspective provides a ground-level roadmap for school leaders to move from abstract technology policy to responsive classroom praxis.

On November 16, 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), working with Mandiant, published findings that mark an important development in the operational use of artificial intelligence in cyber operations. https://x.com/i/status/2123457542345179163 GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework calledexploit_agent. The framework integrated multiple frontier and locally hosted largelanguage models and was configured to continuously analyse software patches, identify potential vulnerabilities, draft exploits and execute them automatically, without human intervention at those stages. This finding moves the discussion of agentic artificial intelligence beyond theoreticalconcerns. The central issue is no longer simply whether AI can generate sophisticated code or assist ahuman attacker. It is whether an AI agent can autonomously transform an objective into asequence of consequential operations, interact with external systems, evaluate executionresults and continue acting at machine speed. This paper examines that development and proposes a different architectural approach:ST-T1024 Agentic Architecture, documented through A1–A16. Its fundamental principle is that an agent may exercise autonomy within a human-definedoperational perimeter, without acquiring authority to redefine that perimeter. The human defines the knowledge library, permissible goals, actions, permissions, execution constraints and verification requirements. The agent operates within those specifications. The proposition is not that autonomous execution must be eliminated. It is that autonomous execution must be separated from autonomous authority. THE AGENT MAY EXECUTE. IT MUST NOT BECOME THE AUTHOR OF ITS OWNAUTHORITY.

Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled more flexible pedagogical interactions in intelligent tutoring systems. However, the reliability of generated content and its impact on actual learning outcomes remain contested. A central research question is how to integrate reliable knowledge with learner states to support tutoring decisions aligned with instructional objectives. Drawing on studies published between 2020 and 2026, this review examines advances in knowledge augmentation and learner modelling, analyses approaches to pedagogical strategy selection and feedback regulation, and assesses existing evidence of educational effectiveness. The literature indicates that retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs can provide a knowledge basis for tutoring responses, while knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis help identify learners' knowledge states. Multi-turn planning and feedback mechanisms also provide greater control over instructional behaviour. Nevertheless, these capabilities have not yet been adequately validated in combination, and improvements in tutoring response quality do not necessarily translate into genuine learning gains. Empirical studies have reported substantially different learning outcomes, suggesting that instructional design and evaluation methods may influence judgements of educational effectiveness. Future research should strengthen the dynamic connections among supporting evidence, learner states, and pedagogical decisions. Independent assessments, knowledge transfer tasks, and longitudinal follow-up are also needed to verify learning outcomes and provide a more robust empirical basis for the design and application of LLM-based intelligent tutoring systems.

documents.abstract: The European Union published the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) in a strategic effort to align the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the common market. This act, one of the first laws of its kind, strengthened the development of trustworthy and human-centered AI through new regulations, prescribing requirements that providers of AI systems must conform to. The Act prescribes model-level technical requirements for high-risk AI systems, such as in terms of accuracy, robustness and fairness, which are to be addressed and reported in the form of conformity assessments. We identify, however, a significant gap between the high-level legal descriptions provided in the law and the low-level requirements needed for the implementation of automated assessment tools for algorithmic auditing. This gap is a major obstacle in the operationalization of AI Act compliance. The difficulties are aggravated due the lack of harmonized AI standards and the existing heterogeneity of AI models, datasets, and tasks. To address this gap, we present an open-source proof-of-concept assessment tool to operationalize the technical requirements of the AI Act according to the current regulatory landscape. With this tool, we demonstrate a bottom-up interpretation of the technical requirements of the AI Act for an automated evaluation of accuracy, robustness, and fairness. We apply our work to two neural network-based healthcare applications and discuss the requirements for further integration to initial conformity assessment and to extended application to post-market monitoring and other algorithmic auditing frameworks. With further work, the base structure presented here can be applied for integration beyond healthcare to other AI high-risk application domains.

documents.abstract: The integration of linguistics and digital educational technologies requires more than adding artificial intelligence (AI) tools to existing language lessons. It requires teachers who can connect linguistic knowledge, pedagogical design, critical evaluation, and responsible technology use. This article proposes a practical framework for AI-supported language teaching in which linguistic analysis becomes the basis for meaningful, context-sensitive learning. The study uses a conceptual and analytical approach, drawing on research into AI in language education, international guidance on teacher AI competencies, and an illustrative teaching sequence built around intertextuality - the way a text draws meaning from other texts and cultural references. The framework includes five stages: identify a language phenomenon, contextualise its function, generate AI-supported alternatives, verify outputs against reliable sources, and evaluate learning through a learner-produced task. The article argues that AI is most educationally valuable when it supports inquiry and feedback rather than replacing teachers’ judgement or learners’ interpretive work. It also outlines risks involving inaccurate explanations, cultural flattening, privacy, bias, and overdependence. The proposed model offers teacher educators a transferable structure for integrating linguistic content with digital tools while maintaining human agency, academic integrity, and clear learning outcomes.

Continuous assessment of human trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally a latent-state identification problem: trust cannot be observed directly, while its behavioral manifestations are noisy, multimodal, and often shared with other internal states such as cognitive load, uncertainty, and attention. This work introduces trustiness as an operational latent variable for characterizing the time-varying trust-related state of a user interacting with an AI system. Rather than treating behavioral measurements as direct proxies for trust, we formulate their relationship with trustiness within a multimodal state-space framework that explicitly separates latent trust, cognitive load, contextual factors, and noisy observations. Candidate gaze, head-motion, and interaction-derived features are characterized through marginal, conditional, and incremental mutual information to determine which observables retain trust-related information after accounting for confounding and multimodal redundancy. The resulting informative observation set is integrated into a recursive latent-state estimator, instantiated through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for continuous inference. In a controlled study with 60 participants, gaze entropy, revisit behavior, verification actions, response latency, and inspection time provided the strongest independent trust-related evidence, while conditioning on cognitive load substantially reduced several otherwise apparent associations. The selected multimodal model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.112, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.149, and a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with self-reported trust across all 60 participants, evaluated on post-calibration interactions after participant-specific Trustiness Calibration Experiment (TCE) calibration. Participants were held out from population-level feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Calibration was conclusive for 57 of 60 participants, for whom the corresponding MAE was 0.108, RMSE was 0.143, and Pearson correlation was 0.81. Joint modeling of trustiness and cognitive load reduced MAE by 18.2% relative to a trustiness-only model in the conclusive-calibration evaluation, while conditional feature selection improved generalization compared with the complete unfiltered observation set. Temporal experiments further showed coherent degradation and recovery of the inferred latent state following controlled changes in AI reliability. These results indicate that continuous trust assessment is better formulated as the identification of a partially observable latent state from confounded multimodal evidence than as direct prediction from behavioral proxies, providing a mathematical framework for multimodal trust estimation in human–AI interaction.

Smartphone video see-through (VST) stylus interaction could support digital ink input on everyday surfaces, reducing reliance on specialised hardware and small screens. Yet the user experience of these systems is not well understood. Unlike writing on paper, users must coordinate a stylus, surface, and display while managing occlusion, stability, surface access, and comfort. We examine user experience through a two-phase study of smartphone VST stylus use. A participatory placement study identified how users intuitively position the phone, stylus, and surface, revealing the handheld position as the most preferred. A usability evaluation of a handheld prototype showed that overall participants found the system to be intuitive to use, with high usability and low workload. These results indicate that stylus VST interaction is a promising way forward for accessible, large-scale, freeform digital input. We contribute design implications for future stylus VST systems including stable repositioning, stylus-position feedback, tracing support, training and ergonomics.

Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants’ accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

documents.abstract: Risk-based quality management (RBQM) is used to help ensure that clinical trial data are fit-for-purpose and that trial quality is protected. RBQM begins by identifying critical-to-quality (CtQ) factors and risks related to such CtQ factors, defining controls such as key risk indicators and data checks, and reviewing data to detect signals. Many organizations can identify signals through centralized monitoring and analytics, but a persistent gap remains in determining whether a signal represents a true issue and what action, if any, is appropriate given study data and site context.The authors met as a cross-functional group with experience in clinical data management, statistics, quality, clinical operations, and clinical trial technology. Participants represented both sponsor and service provider organizations and brought practical experience from active trials. The group met to discuss how RBQM is applied today and how organizations might better move from identified signals to appropriate, data-supported actions.This paper presents a consensus view of the capabilities needed to close this gap. The group concluded that agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is unlikely to be useful in this setting unless it is grounded in structured study context, well-understood data, and an issue management process. Neither statistical analysis nor AI can establish causality; what they can do is focus attention and support structured investigation so that study teams can determine the underlying reason for a signal and decide on an appropriate action. The capabilities described here are offered as design considerations for the field rather than as an endorsement of any product or implementation.

Digital transformation is increasingly experienced not as a bounded program of organizational change but as a condition of recurrent and overlapping adaptation. Research has clarified many technological, strategic, and employee-level consequences of this shift, yet it has paid less attention to a leadership-specific problem: the possibility that leaders can continue to look effective while progressively losing the cognitive, emotional, temporal, and recovery resources required to remain effective. This conceptual paper develops a leadership-specific process theory of quiet cracking under continuous digital transformation. Rather than claiming a wholly new strain construct, the paper refines the emerging quiet-cracking literature by specifying a distinctive leadership configuration in which preserved short-term role enactment coexists with hidden resource erosion. Conservation of Resources theory provides the primary explanatory engine, while role theory, Job Demands-Resources theory, compensatory-control theory, emotional-labor research, recovery theory, and Restricted Employee Sustainability Theory are integrated to explain the process. The model proposes that continuous digital transformation intensity generates experienced transformation load; that resource loss and institutionalized recovery deficits translate this load into leadership quiet cracking; and that the dual position of leaders as change recipients and change agents, together with change-champion emotional labor, accelerates depletion. Compensatory effort can preserve visible performance and create a detection lag between internal deterioration and external failure. Adaptive leadership resilience and recovery-supportive organizational resources can slow this trajectory, but persistent overload can produce a resilience-masking loop in which resilient performance delays corrective action until buffering capacity saturates. The paper contributes a temporal and role-specific explanation of hidden leader deterioration and positions human sustainability as a boundary condition of digital agility.

As deep learning models grow in size and complexity, optimizing the execution efficiency becomes critical. Operator fusion merges multiple operators to reduce memory overhead and enhance computational efficiency. However, the combinatorial explosion of possible fusion combinations in modern models creates a search space that challenges traditional manual and heuristic methods. We propose FusionAdvisor, a neural network based framework that predicts the speedups of candidate fusion strategies from computation graphs and recommends the top- candidates (recommended strategies). Trained on our constructed fusion strategy dataset, it abstracts fusion selection as a service, enabling developers to choose high-performance strategies and accelerate inference efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that FusionAdvisor’s neural network predicts post-fusion speedups with low error, enabling promising strategy recommendations while maintaining search efficiency comparable to the existing methods. This work advances automated operator fusion selection, reduces optimization costs, and improves resource utilization in complex scenarios, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and other large-scale models.

documents.abstract: In safety-critical interactive spaces, such as flight decks, pilots must be able to maintain a forward-facing visual attention to monitor primary instruments, current weather, or other aircraft. However, typical flight decks require interaction with switches that are located outside the pilot’s view. Short, well-practiced glances at controls are part of normal cockpit operation. Longer shifts of attention away from the monitoring task to locate controls can cause problematic situations, including unnoticed changes in surrounding traffic and flight path deviations. In physical cockpits, pilots can safely rely on haptic and tactile features to select a control without looking. However, as modern pilot training increasingly transitions to Virtual Reality Flight Simulations (VRFS) to reduce costs, this crucial tactile reference is lost. Without this tactile reference in Virtual Reality (VR), trainees rely on visual guidance during switch selection, which can divert attention from the monitoring task. To resolve these VRFS-related limitations, we introduce and evaluate two techniques that enable monitoring while interacting in VR using gaze-preserving peripheral views: an orthographic ( V Ortho ) and a perspective-correct ( V Persp ) representation of the corresponding cockpit panel. Furthermore, we present a dynamic height indicator to help users determine the remaining distance between the virtual fingertip and the desired cockpit element. In a within-subjects study, 28 participants with no aviation experience compared both techniques with an unassisted baseline in a high-fidelity VR Boeing 737-800 cockpit. Our findings show that both views successfully lower error rates on the monitoring task. However, this benefit comes with trade-offs: both views increase task completion times and subjective workload (as measured by NASA-TLX). The number of missed switches, normalized path error (NPE), and pre- to post-study SSQ scores showed no notable degradation, indicating that users adapted well to the peripheral views without adverse effects.

Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. GCP is compatible by translation: it consumes Poppy identity and session credentials, maps its catalog/cart/checkout objects to UCP and ACP, and carries GCP-specific safety and authorization fields as extension namespaces. We specify the protocol, give a reference implementation and conformance suite, and introduce AutomotiveCommerce-Bench, 60 tasks across parts, merchandise, after-sales service, and insurance/reservation, with hidden compatibility, safety, authorization, and exception traps. In a real-LLM study with three models, GCP raises task success from 64.5% (manual web) and 69.4% (generic agent commerce) to 92.2%, cuts misbuy from 35.5%/30.6% to 7.8%, and raises exception recovery from about 58% to 89.6%, while a calibrated human model achieves 68-83% success in 8-25 minutes per task. We also compare agent commerce with a calibrated model of human shopping behavior and show where the protocol changes the error, time, and authorization trade-off. Beyond the benchmark, a Stripe test-mode sandbox (180 charges, 180/180 reconciled) shows that bounded delegation cuts human approvals by 70% relative to per-transaction approval with no loss of success, and a semi-field study on real catalogs shows no degradation. In a cockpit simulation, GCP reduces unsafe driving-time purchase attempts from 47.9% to 0% (deferral rises to 81.2%), and on a real aftermarket parts/service-kit catalog it raises success from 26.7% to 100%. We also lay out a near-term interaction horizon (12-24 months), from assisted commerce to delegated and agent-native commerce, and derive the protocol requirements each horizon creates. The protocol, benchmark, and all raw results are released.

University students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in their everyday learning. This study used the value-based adoption model (VAM), extended with subjective norm, to examine students’ perceived value of these tools and its relationship with intention to pay. Questionnaire data from 309 Chinese university students were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Perceived usefulness, perceived price, and subjective norm showed significant positive associations with perceived value. Higher perceived value was also significantly associated with stronger payment intentions. The paths from perceived enjoyment, perceived risk, and perceived ease of use to perceived value were not statistically significant. The results support using VAM to study payment intentions for GenAI learning tools and have implications for tool design and university guidance on their use.

documents.abstract: Recently, vision-language pretraining has emerged as a transformative technique that integrates the strengths of both visual and textual modalities, resulting in powerful vision-language models (VLMs). Leveraging web-scale pretraining data, these models exhibit strong zero-shot capabilities. However, their performance often deteriorates when confronted with domain-specific or specialized generalization tasks. To address this, a growing body of research focuses on transferring or generalizing the rich knowledge embedded in VLMs to various downstream applications. This survey aims to comprehensively summarize the generalization settings, methodologies, benchmarking, and results in VLM literatures. Delving into the typical VLM structures, current literatures are categorized into prompt-based , parameter-based , and feature-based methods according to the transferred modules. The differences and characteristics in each category are further summarized and discussed by revisiting the typical transfer learning (TL) settings , providing novel interpretations for TL in the era of VLMs. Popular benchmarks for VLM generalization are further introduced with thorough performance comparisons among the reviewed methods. Following the advances in large-scale generalizable pretraining, this survey also discusses the relations and differences between VLMs and up-to-date multimodal large language models (MLLM), e.g., DeepSeek-VL. By systematically reviewing the surging literatures in vision-language research from a novel and practical generalization prospective, this survey contributes to a clear landscape of current and future multimodal researches.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become common workplace infrastructure faster than almost any digital technology before it, moving from experimental novelty to everyday workplace infrastructure, yet a critical question remains underexplored in the Indian organisational context: do GenAI tools actually make employees perform better or does that depend on something else entirely – how digitally competent the employee already is? We examine whether digital competence is the missing link in explaining when and for whom the adoption of Generative AI translates into measurable performance gains. Data were collected from 500 employees working in multinational companies located in major Indian business hubs of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram/NCR, Mumbai and Chennai using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design. The suggested model Generative AI Adoption → Digital Competence → Employee Performance was tested using a full analytical pipeline, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s Alpha, Composite Reliability (CR), Average Variance Extracted (AVE), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), correlation analysis, independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, multiple regression, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and bootstrapped mediation analysis. The Findings (reported here on an illustrative dataset, to be replaced by the primary data) suggest that the adoption of Generative AI is significantly and positively associated with digital competence, that digital competence is significantly and positively associated with employee performance, and that digital competence partially mediates the relationship between the adoption of GenAI and performance. The T-test and ANOVA results also suggest that the strength of this chain varies significantly by sex, organisational tenure and job role, indicating a more nuanced, skills-dependent adoption story rather than a homogenous productivity dividend. The findings suggest that Indian subsidiaries of multinationals should focus on digital-competence development, rather than just tool deployment, as the strategic lever to convert GenAI investment into performance results, with a particular focus on tenure-based and role-based upskilling gaps. The current study is among the first integrated SEM-based tests of digital competence as a mediating mechanism in the GenAI–performance relationship within India’s multinational corporate workforce, a fast-growing, strategically important, yet empirically under-examined segment of the global GenAI adoption story.

Background In fragile, post-conflict economies facing severe youth unemployment, digital freelancing offers an essential pathway to economic self-reliance. This study investigates how Generative AI Competence (GAIC) drives Freelance Digital Skill Augmentation (FDSA) and Platform Market Competitiveness (PMC) to enhance Student Freelance Income Generation (SFIG), while assessing the moderating impact of Structural, Financial, and Institutional Barriers (SFIB) in Somalia. Methods Drawing on Augmented Human Capital Theory, Platform Labor Theory, and the Capability Approach, a cross-sectional survey collected primary empirical data from N = 415 active university student freelancers across Mogadishu, Hargeisa, Garowe, and Kismayo. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, psychometric validation, and interaction moderation analyses. Results Generative AI Competence exerts significant positive direct effects on Freelance Digital Skill Augmentation (β = 0.548, p < 0.001) and Platform Market Competitiveness (β = 0.312, p < 0.001). Digital skill augmentation strongly predicts Student Freelance Income Generation (β = 0.384, p < 0.001) and mediates GenAI's economic impact. However, structural barriers significantly dampen this conversion (β = -0.198, p < 0.001), causing a 68.0% drop in income velocity under high-barrier conditions. International payment exclusion (lack of PayPal/Stripe) and platform KYC geoblocking are identified as the most severe institutional constraints. The model explains 61.4% of variance in student freelance income (R² = 0.614). Conclusions Generative AI serves as a powerful leapfrogging mechanism that mitigates local pedagogical voids and enhances global market access for youth in fragile economies. Nevertheless, technological competence alone cannot overcome structural exclusion. Developing accessible cross-border payment gateways and resolving platform geoblocking are urgent imperatives to unlock Somalia's digital youth dividend.

The growing diffusion of renewable energy sources, storage systems, and distributed energy resources is fostering a transformation in electricity markets, characterized by increasingly active participation by end users. In this context, peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading models enable producers, consumers, and prosumers to exchange energy within energy communities and local systems, introducing new methods of negotiation and resource management. This paper analyzes the contribution of generative artificial intelligence, with particular reference to large language models (LLMs), to the automation of decision-making processes in P2P energy markets. The review adopts a targeted narrative approach, covering recent literature together with selected foundational studies, and organizes the evidence according to LLM roles in forecasting, trading and negotiation, MARL-assisted decision making, and hybrid architectures. The analysis focuses on automated trading, bidding and negotiation strategies, LLM–MARL integration, and complementary technologies such as blockchain, smart contracts, forecasting, and storage management. The reviewed evidence suggests that current architectures are most credible when LLMs support interpretation, strategy generation, and higher-level decisions, while network feasibility, market clearing, settlement, and other safety-critical functions remain assigned to deterministic or otherwise verifiable modules.

Waste management has become a growing environmental concern in this modern era, particularly due to the increasing amount of waste generated by household activities. In 2020, Indonesia generated approximately 67.8 million tons of waste, with 37.3% originating from households. This study aims to design a prototype of ReVive, an application for buying and selling reusable second-hand goods as an alternative approach to reducing household waste accumulation. The study employed the Design Thinking method with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (AI), specifically ChatGPT, through five stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. The resulting ReVive prototype provides functionalities for buying and selling reusable second-hand goods. The prototype was evaluated using the System Usability Scale (SUS) involving prospective users. The evaluation resulted in an average SUS score of 74.88, indicating that the prototype achieved an excellent level of usability. The findings also indicate that generative AI can support and facilitate activities throughout the Design Thinking process, particularly during the development of design ideas and prototypes. ReVive therefore offers an alternative digital solution for promoting the reuse of household goods and reducing the potential accumulation of household waste.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being adopted in education, yet its application to physics remains challenging because of the discipline’s reliance on mathematical, symbolic, and multimodal reasoning. This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic mapping review of 146 studies published between January 2023 and June 2026 on the use of GenAI in physics education. The review examines the research landscape, approaches for supporting students and teachers, and methods for benchmarking and improving GenAI systems. The findings reveal rapid growth in research activity with widespread but uneven geographic distribution, with most studies focusing on higher education and relying heavily on third-party GenAI services. Student-support research primarily addresses conversational tutoring and personalized guidance, while teacher-support studies focus on lesson planning and teaching material development, professional development and teacher perceptions. A substantial body of work also benchmarks GenAI performance on physics-related tasks or proposes methods for improving it. Overall, the reviewed literature demonstrates considerable potential for GenAI in physics education while highlighting the need for further research on multilingual and inclusive systems, specialized educational uses, privacy-preserving approaches, improved multimodal support, and integration with complementary educational technologies.

documents.abstract: Article 7¹ of the Law "On Informatization" of the Republic of Uzbekistan prohibits basing legally significant decisions solely on the output of artificial intelligence. Article 24 of the Law "On Personal Data" still permits solely automated decisions with the subject's consent or for the performance of a contract, and in lending these two exceptions cover almost every application. The borrower's protection therefore depends on what the law will accept as real human involvement and on what the bank must tell the applicant. The paper proposes four criteria of genuine human control over a credit decision and argues that the use of AI in assessing creditworthiness creates a pre-contractual duty of the bank to inform the applicant. It ends with a proposal for Article 65¹ of the Law "On Banks and Banking Activity" and for a clarification by the Plenum of the Supreme Court.

The deployment of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) within complex physical systems remains a grand challenge. While intelligent manufacturing aims to address this by infusing industrial processes with real-time adaptation, the prevailing approach often involves applying machine learning (ML) to isolated, well-defined sub-problems. This component-wise strategy, however, proves insufficient for processes like wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), where geometric fidelity is governed by deeply coupled, multi-scale thermo-fluid dynamics that defy simple predictive modelling. Here, using WAAM as a foundational case study of a complex cyber-physical system, we provide a systematic review of the intelligent strategies required for end-to-end geometry control. We deconstruct this challenge into a unified framework spanning the full process chain—pre-deposition, in-process, and post-deposition—and map the corresponding control methods onto the critical physical scales of the bead, layer, and part. Our synthesis reveals that the primary limitations are not a lack of algorithmic novelty but rather fundamental issues of model generalisation from sparse, high-cost data and the integration of heterogeneous physical priors. This analysis points towards a necessary paradigm shift: moving from static, data-driven prediction towards dynamic, autonomous control architectures. We argue that realising the next generation of intelligent manufacturing requires a focus on integrated systems, such as physics-informed digital twins and multi-sensor fusion platforms, that can holistically manage process complexity in real time.

Geometry is important because it trains spatial reasoning and is fundamental to many STEM subjects. However, many students struggle to connect the symbolic formulas of geometry and linear algebra to the spatial relationships they describe. We present GeoScratch, a web application in which students solve geometry problems by composing a Scratch-style block-based language against a live 3D scene, rather than by manipulating formulas. By separating spatial reasoning from symbolic notation in this way, we aim to reduce cognitive load and make the subject more approachable for students with mathematics anxiety. A within-subjects study with 29 university STEM students, comparing GeoScratch to conventional lecture slides, showed that learning gains for both methods were similar. GeoScratch received above-neutral scores for the subscales Interest/Enjoyment, Perceived Competence, and Value/Usefulness of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory. Participants judged GeoScratch as supporting both intuitive and formulaic understanding above neutral.

Cubes are increasingly used in tangible interaction, particularly when arranged in a topology on a surface such as a tabletop. To better understand how end users manipulate cubes as gestural input for tangible interaction on a surface, we report empirical findings from a family of three experiments conducted with AudioCubes , a set of tangible cubes containing wireless computers with built-in sound and signal generating and processing capabilities that sense their topology for four action types on a surface: positioning, moving, rotating, and arranging. The two first experiments investigate the usability of AudioCubes through a controlled study with and without an active training, inside and outside a laboratory. The third experiment determines which gestures are spontaneously produced by end users in an uncontrolled study and how they articulate these gestures by fingers. Tangible cubes offer a usable and intuitive medium for gestural interaction. Participants consistently favored face-based interactions over edges and corners, simpler one-to-one mappings over complex multi-object procedures, and physically stable arrangements over precision-dependent gestures. Usable cube interfaces should prioritize grasping, pushing, rotating, and aligning through cube faces, while minimizing reliance on corner-based or highly constrained actions. The actual composition of cubes covers only 32% of the theoretical space of 169 spatial compositions. Some practical implications for designing gestural input with tangible cubes on a surface, such as a tabletop, are offered.

Advances in Autonomous GIS have demonstrated that geospatial agents can plan, generate, and execute GIS workflows from natural language input. Existing systems, however, focus more on workflow execution tasks such as geospatial code generation and spatial analysis. Less attention has been given to how autonomous GIS systems can support broader stages of geospatial scientific inquiry. This paper presents a multi-agent co-scientist framework for autonomous geospatial scientific inquiry. The framework distributes scientific responsibilities across six specialized agents responsible for research question understanding, geospatial data retrieval, planning, spatial modeling, result analysis, and reporting. These agents operate through a shared context module and reproducibility layer, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at stages where geographic judgment substantially affects downstream analysis. We implement the framework as GIS Co-Scientist, a web-based prototype, and demonstrate it through three research examples. Across the three cases, the system successfully generated research plans and analytical workflows, executed spatial models, produced draft manuscripts, preserved full workflow provenance, and supported iterative post-hoc revision of analytical steps with human feedback. The framework advances autonomous GIS for geographic knowledge discovery and clarifies how autonomy and human authorship can be designed as complementary properties of scientific systems.

Background The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine triggered one of the largest and most rapid displacement crises in recent history, creating sustained challenges for refugee protection, data coordination, and healthcare delivery. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods study integrating longitudinal displacement data from international, governmental, and secondary sources with a systematic analysis of 51 healthcare policy documents and reports from ten major host countries. Quantitative analyses examined temporal and geographic displacement patterns, cross-source reporting discrepancies, and admission pathways. Large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction with independent human validation identified and assessed frequent domains in healthcare access across host countries. Results Ukrainian displacement remained protracted through 2025 and increasingly shifted from neighboring countries toward Western Europe, with Germany becoming the largest host country from 2024. Refugee estimates varied substantially across sources, likely because of differences in definitions, reference periods, and counting methods. The U.S. response relied primarily on humanitarian parole and temporary protection rather than formal refugee resettlement. LLM-assisted analysis identified five healthcare access domains: registration, primary care, mental health, specialist care, and additional services. Across the ten host countries, access ranged from comprehensive in Germany, the Netherlands, and Spain to highly constrained in Moldova. Major barriers included language difficulties, administrative complexity, financial constraints, geographic disparities, and limited healthcare navigation. Mental health and psychosocial services remained insufficient. Conclusions Formal protection and healthcare eligibility did not ensure equitable access. Harmonized refugee-data standards, durable legal pathways, professional interpretation, multilingual navigation, and expanded mental health, telehealth, and mobile services are needed to strengthen current and future humanitarian responses.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Manual chart review remains the primary method of clinical data collection in spine surgery research but is time intensive and prone to human error. Large language models may enable automated extraction of clinically meaningful events from unstructured operative text. We evaluated the performance of generative pre-trained transformer 4 (GPT-4) in detecting intraoperative adverse events from spine surgery operative notes compared with trained human reviewers. METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 1454 laminectomy cases performed at a single academic institution between 2016 and 2022 was analyzed. Deidentified operative notes were independently reviewed by 4 trained human reviewers and GPT-4 using standardized prompts to identify incidental durotomy and nondurotomy intraoperative adverse events. Discordant classifications were adjudicated by a senior reviewer to establish ground truth. Performance metrics including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and F1 score were calculated. Analyses were stratified by operative note length, and review time was estimated. RESULTS: Incidental durotomy occurred in 88 cases (6.1%). GPT-4 achieved 100.0% sensitivity compared with 89.8% for human reviewers, with lower positive predictive value (88.0% vs 100.0%) but similar specificity (99.1% vs 100.0%). For nondurotomy adverse events (n = 21), GPT-4 demonstrated higher sensitivity than humans (90.5% vs 57.1%) with equivalent specificity (100.0%). GPT-4 maintained stable performance across note length quartiles, whereas human reviewer sensitivity decreased for longer notes. Human reviewers required approximately 35 hours to review all notes, compared with approximately 2 hours for GPT-4. CONCLUSION: GPT-4 demonstrated higher observed sensitivity than trained human reviewers for detecting intraoperative adverse events from spine surgery operative reports while reducing review time by more than 90%. Large language model-assisted chart review may serve as a scalable human-in-the-loop adjunct to traditional chart review, improving the completeness and efficiency of neurosurgical outcomes research.

Just-In-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) increasingly rely on conversational agents to elicit user routines, yet translating fluid human dialogue into rigid schedule data remains a significant challenge. We conducted a qualitative investigation of a neurosymbolic pipeline, combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with a Neo4j knowledge graph, to map unstructured verbal narratives into actionable interventions. Through human-centric evaluation using natural-language playbacks, we identified a critical “mental-model gap,” where the linear extraction of LLMs clashes with hierarchical, non-linear human storytelling, causing severe entity fragmentation. Furthermore, we articulate an “ecological mismatch,” demonstrating that algorithmic schedule availability frequently ignores the user’s fluctuating psychological receptivity and physical energy levels. To resolve these tensions, we propose actionable design heuristics, including routine piggybacking, adaptive negotiation, and scalable transparency. Ultimately, these guidelines provide a foundational framework for evolving rigid schedule-trackers into empathetic, context-aware proactive agents capable of supporting long-term health behavior change.

In many real-world scenarios, users interact with digital systems while their hands are partially occupied, such as when holding tools or everyday objects. Prior work on busy-hand interaction has focused on microgestures and motion-based techniques, which rely on finger articulation or relative movement. In situations where a stable grasp is required, such as handling fragile, heavy, or precision objects, such motion can be undesirable or impractical. Pressure-based input offers a complementary modality that enables interaction without changing finger pose, yet its use while holding objects has received limited empirical attention. To explore this, we conducted two within-subject experiments examining users’ ability to perform controlled pressure selections and analyzing finger-specific performance across different grasps and geometries. Results indicate that participants can reliably perform pressure-based selections in these conditions, achieving high success rates (92.7% on average) with low selection times (1.74s on average). Our findings characterize the potential of pressure input as a complementary microinteraction modality under grasp-constrained, busy-hand scenarios.

This integrative literature review asks how external pressures and organizational capabilities combine to support green innovation and multidimensional sustainable performance in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). A transparent audit of the manuscript bibliography identified 62 cited entries; removing two duplicates and separating three institutional reports yielded 57 distinct scholarly sources for citation-based thematic synthesis, with recent evidence emphasized and seminal theory retained. The analysis compares external drivers, capability formation, product and process innovation, environmental and economic outcomes, digital complementarity, and contextual constraints. Across the reviewed evidence, stakeholder pressure and regulation are more likely to stimulate innovation when knowledge management, absorptive capacity, leadership, and green dynamic capabilities support implementation. Environmental gains are more consistent than short-term financial returns; firm size, financing, readiness, industry, and commercialization shape the variation. Digitalization and artificial intelligence are treated as conditional enabling capabilities, not automatic performance drivers. Drawing primarily on dynamic capability theory, the review proposes a six-stage green capability cycle that connects sensing, mobilization, innovation, measurement, learning, and resource reconfiguration. The cycle is a literature-informed conceptual proposition requiring longitudinal validation, not an empirically tested causal model.

documents.abstract: How does an aircraft verify which AI agent may request what — and prove every interaction afterwards? GUARDAID Annex 9 adapts the GUARDAID open standard for aviation systems. Instead of hardcoding mission rules, the standard defines cryptographically signed configuration slots: the aircraft operator and the manufacturer each fill their own slots to declare who holds command authority, which action verbs a principal's agent may issue, how the aircraft behaves during a data-link loss, and which alert policies govern operations. The specification supplies the structure and verification tools; the aircraft owner supplies the policy values. By design, the protocol never drives flight actuators—actuator requests are blocked structurally, while every telemetry reading is logged and sealed in a tamper-evident trail.The deposit includes the complete reference reader and reproducible verification suite: a deterministic generator producing 209 test cases and 224 presentations with byte-identical outputs on every run, plus 159 adversarial mutations, all detected. Validated across nine rounds of independent hostile audit and cross-checked by a separate verifier.Scope notice: This technical note is not an airworthiness certification; physical test-bench qualification and safety assessments remain the responsibility of the applicant.本附件将GUARDAID开放标准应用于航空领域:运营方与制造方各自填写签名的配置槽,标准只提供结构与工具,不直接控制任何执行机构。附带可完全复现的参考读取器:209个测试用例、159项变异测试全部检出,并经九轮独立审计。本文件不构成适航认证;物理测试台与安全评估由申请方负责。

Touch interaction on everyday surfaces has long been envisioned as an extension of mixed-reality input, offering tactile feedback and proprioceptive cues that enhance user comfort and precision. However, most existing mixed-reality touch-sensing techniques are designed for static, dry, and large surfaces, making them unsuitable for real-world use where surfaces may be handheld, wet, or smaller in size. We introduce HaloTouch++, a mixed-reality touch input technique that enables low lift-off, water-tolerant and finger profile modified interactions on handheld surfaces. The system harnesses multi-path interference from time-of-flight depth sensing as a stable optical cue for detecting physical contact. A lightweight, plastic reflector attached to the surface amplifies these interference patterns, forming a distinctive “Halo” signature around touch points that remains consistent across surfaces and under varying poses and moisture conditions. In a 15-participant evaluation spanning multiple materials, user poses, and water conditions, HaloTouch++ achieved 97.3% touch-down accuracy and 93.3% gesture recognition accuracy.

Virtual Reality (VR) offers the potential for productivity work by providing expansive workspaces anywhere, yet supporting bare-hand interaction with multiple 2D windows remains challenging. We present HandPad, an asymmetric bimanual interaction framework that combines differentiated hand roles, self-haptic interaction, and hand remapping for multi-window interaction. The non-dominant hand sets a spatial frame, selects the interaction context, and provides a self-haptic surface, while the dominant hand performs on-hand touch and complementary mid-air manipulation relative to that frame. HandPad organizes interaction into three modes supporting cross-window navigation, within-window content manipulation, and application-window management. It also remaps the physical hands to virtual windows, allowing users to interact from more flexible physical postures regardless of window location. An exploratory study suggests that HandPad provides coherent interaction workflows, while revealing design tradeoffs between on-hand and mid-air interaction, informing the design of future bimanual interfaces for multi-window VR workspaces.

documents.abstract: Health and care settings present high-stakes contexts where it is essential that decision-making and access to information are timely and accurate. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools is increasingly influencing practice, while also introducing risks and challenges that can affect the safety, fairness, and trustworthiness of AI systems in these settings. This workshop critically explores the use of AI tools in health and care settings through the prism of four dimensions: power, time, inclusion and emotions. It will explore how pushing the boundaries of scenarios on the edge can influence the lived experience of multiple stakeholders, including healthcare providers, caregivers, researchers, industry partners, and people accessing health and care services. Participants will share experiences of AI use in health and care settings, engage in scenarios that can be challenged by the four dimensions, and reflect on how technology design can be sensitised to address the risks and challenges raised by the four dimensions in situations on the edge.
