Background and objectives Hemoglobinopathies, including beta thalassemia, are blood disorders caused by mutations in the HBB gene. Accurate and early screening of heterozygous carriers is necessary to prevent mutations from being transmitted to offspring. Diagnosis of carrier status is based on hemoglobin A2 (HbA2) and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, requiring expensive equipment for quantification. This work aims to develop machine learning models for prediction of HbA2 and HbF from routine blood test parameters in persons with hemoglobinopathies and normal individuals. Methods Mixture of Experts (MoE) approach was applied to develop the models using an Indian dataset of 5314 individuals. Post-hoc interpretations were obtained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). An affinity-based classifier was developed to predict the diagnostic labels from the predicted HbA2 and HbF. Finally, a web application, HemoPred, was developed as frontend of the models. Results MoE models achieved mean absolute errors of 0.1654 and 0.1394, and R 2 -scores of 0.8442 and 0.6055 for HbA2 and HbF prediction, respectively, with 5-fold cross-validation. The models achieved similar performance in held-out internal validation. SHAP revealed MCV, MCH, and RDW-CV as top contributors. Affinity-based classifier achieved 95% top-2-accuracy (5-fold cross-validation) in multiclass prediction. In binary (disease/normal) classification, it achieved 77% balanced accuracy with 93% sensitivity. HemoPred is available at https://aihemo.mp.aau.dk/hemopred . Conclusions ML models developed for HbA2 and HbF prediction, and diagnostic classification from the predicted HbA2 and HbF can aid doctors. This work is limited by unavailable multi-center data for external validation and unmeasured confounders, including nutritional profiles and α-thalassemia co-inheritance status.

Reflective practice helps learners make sense of early-career workplace experiences, but can be difficult to sustain amid ambiguity, vulnerability, and pressure to present oneself competently. As AI tools are proposed as scalable supports, their implications for learner authority remain underexplored. This study examined AI-supported reflection in early-career workplace learning through a two-week design probe with five tertiary students and recent graduates undertaking placements, internships, or graduate programs. Participants completed spoken, written, structured, and AI-mediated reflection activities alongside mood tracking. Data comprised probe artefacts, AI outputs, and interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis and a multidimensional framework. Participants valued AI for organising thoughts, offering perspectives, and supporting communication, but resisted it when AI authored reflections, inferred emotions, or interpreted meaning. We propose conditional scaffolding: AI supports reflection when learners retain authority over meaning-making. We discuss implications for flexible scaffolds, bounded AI roles, temporal pattern visibility, and connections to human reflection.

Smart homes with ambient sensors record daily life continuously and privately, underpinning aging-in-place monitoring and ambient intelligence. Yet for two decades such systems have produced only discrete activity labels, which cannot express concurrent, ambiguous, or transitional behaviour; roughly half of all recorded data collapses into an uninformative “Other” class. We present HomeNarrator, to our knowledge the first system to generate free-text descriptions of resident activity from binary PIR and door sensors. It converts raw CASAS events into structured elapsed-time segments, which a large language model (LLM) narrates under evidence-bounded rules that limit hallucination. Lacking reference descriptions, we evaluate reference-free: a three-model LLM jury, cross-validated against human annotators, scores each description on an evidence-grounded rubric. In the stratified annotation subset, raters judged 78 % of windows high quality (mean nine or above), and the jury tracked that mean within one point (MAE 0.76 / 0.84). These results establish descriptive human activity recognition (HAR) as feasible on sparse ambient sensors in single-resident homes.

documents.abstract: Human oversight is widely required for autonomous and artificial-intelligence systems, yet assigning a human role does not establish that the person can influence a hazardous trajectory. This study develops a bounded Safety-Control Governance Framework for assessing whether documentary human-control claims are operationally inspectable. Drawing on systems-theoretic safety, supervisory control, situation awareness, resilience engineering, meaningful human control, and AI governance, the framework distinguishes seven operational functions—authority allocation, feedback and observability, situational comprehension, intervention timing, safe-state objective, escalation, and recovery—and two cross-cutting governance functions: accountability assignment and documentation or assurance. The framework was applied to a purposive corpus of 24 public documents spanning autonomous mobility, maritime autonomy, drones and emergency operations, and high-risk AI or command support, producing 216 document–function observations. Authority and accountability were Explicit in 20 of 24 documents and documentation or assurance in 23 of 24. Explicit specification was less frequent for intervention timing (8 of 22 known cases), safe-state objectives (7 of 23), escalation (10 of 24), and recovery (6 of 24). Documentary families supplied complementary evidence, while configuration analysis located distinct discontinuities, including explicit authority while feedback and comprehension were not both Explicit in ten documents. Most degradation-pattern evidence was anticipatory or prescriptive rather than event-based. These numerical profiles are conditional on the final coding rules and source selection. The framework provides an evidence-linked protocol for tracing documentary control gaps; it does not assess operational performance.

Sedentary office environments contribute to flexibility loss and musculoskeletal disorders. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers scalable rehabilitation, its clinical reasoning and biomechanical safety remain scrutinized in academic literature. This study compared the efficacy of 15-minute home-based flexibility exercises designed by human experts versus those generated by AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro) on flexibility, lower back health, and muscle stiffness. In this quasi-randomized controlled trial, 30 male participants were allocated to a Human Expert Group ( n = 15) or an AI Group ( n = 15) using a random start (single coin toss) followed by alternating allocation, which differed from the wording of the ethics-approved application (simple random method, coin toss) and carries a risk of selection bias. Interventions lasted 4 weeks (3 days/week). Assessments included Sit-and-Reach tests, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and MyotonPRO stiffness measurements. Initially, the groups exhibited similar characteristics ( p > .05). In the Sit-and-Reach test, a measure of flexibility, the average score for the human expert group increased from 14.93 ± 10.67 cm to 22.60 ± 11.49 cm, while in the artificial intelligence group, this value reached only from 16.23 ± 7.91 to 17.53 ± 7.60 cm; a statistically significant Time × Group interaction with a large effect size was detected between the groups (F(1,28) = 28.26, p < .001, ηp² = 0.502). A significant Time × Group interaction was also found for the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) (F(1,28) = 7.49, p = .011, ηp² = 0.211). Following Benjamini–Hochberg False Discovery Rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity adjustment across the eight interaction tests, statistically significant Time × Group interactions robustly survived for Sit-and-Reach flexibility ( p < .001), Oswestry Disability Index ( p = .011), dominant biceps femoris stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.01, p = .003, ηp² = 0.282), and non-dominant gastrocnemius stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.16, p = .002, ηp² = 0.285) in favor of the human expert group. In contrast, the Time × Group interaction for dominant erector spinae stiffness was nominally significant prior to adjustment only (F(1,28) = 4.41, raw p = .045, ηp² = 0.136) and did not survive FDR correction. No significant interactions were observed for the remaining muscle groups ( p > .05). Based on the observed Time × Group interaction effects, human expert-generated programs containing dynamic and static flexibility exercises yielded significantly greater improvement over time in flexibility and lower-back health than the single-shot static stretching program generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro. These findings highlight the short-term efficacy of the specific expert-designed dynamic protocol rather than demonstrating a generalized limitation of generative AI in exercise prescription. Trial registration : The study was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov under the number NCT07242287. (Date of Registration 11/17/2025)

Maritime accidents arise from interactions among people, work organisation, technology and the operating environment. Although casualty analyses frequently code human-related contributors, these classifications should not be interpreted as evidence that individual seafarers are the predominant root cause of accidents. This integrative narrative review therefore examines human factors as manifestations of a wider socio-technical system. A structured two-layer review strategy was used. Twenty maritime-focused empirical, review and analytical sources formed the core evidence corpus, while supplementary theoretical and cross-domain sources were used only to interpret mechanisms and transfer preventive lessons. The core synthesis identified four recurring patterns: fatigue and cognitive strain are shaped by scheduling, recovery opportunities, noise and automation demands; communication problems in multinational crews extend beyond language to authority gradients and shared mental models; reporting behaviour is strongly conditioned by organisational climate, commercial pressure and regulatory implementation; and many apparently individual errors emerge from interactions across cognitive, team, organisational, technical and environmental levels. HFACS, the Swiss Cheese Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Groupthink Theory, Error Management Theory, Rasmussen’s socio-technical perspective and Safety-II are therefore treated as complementary interpretive lenses rather than competing explanations. A preventive diagnostic matrix is proposed to connect analytical level, observable risk conditions, assessment indicators and upstream interventions. The review argues that maritime safety management should move away from worker-centred error correction toward primary prevention that redesigns work, technology, leadership and reporting systems around the conditions that shape safe performance.

Managers in nonprofit and non-governmental organisations increasingly receive advice from artificial intelligence tools when they forecast demand, allocate staff and budgets, screen applications, prioritise programmes and assess risk. The central management question is no longer whether such advice is available but how human judgement should be combined with it. This conceptual paper develops a calibrated-judgement framework for AI-assisted management decisions. It builds on two experimental literatures that point in different directions. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey report that people became less likely to rely on an algorithm after seeing it err, even when it outperformed a human forecaster. Alon-Barkat and Busuioc, in three experiments in the Netherlands, found no evidence of automation bias but found stronger adherence to advice aligned with group stereotypes in one study, with no significant difference between algorithmic and human-expert advice. These findings are connected to research on accountability and advice rationales, conditions for intuitive expertise, complacency and automation bias, decision structures and the automation–augmentation paradox. The framework holds that reliance on AI advice should be calibrated to the predictability of the decision environment, the reasons given for advice and the accountability that attaches to the decision. Six propositions address advice rationales, track records, selective adherence, workload, decision structure and skill preservation. No original empirical data are presented.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive trade analytics, and multimodal generative models into multinational enterprise (MNE) operations has fundamentally disrupted the foundational assumptions of International Business (IB) higher education. Traditional IB pedagogy—anchored in static comparative advantage models, retrospective case analyses, and isolated cross-cultural taxonomies—increasingly fails to prepare graduates for an era defined by algorithmic global value chains and geopolitical fragmentation. Moving beyond superficial classroom tool adoption, this study investigates how Artificial Intelligence can systematically restructure International Business education through the theoretical lenses of Institutional Entrepreneurship, Distributed Cognition, and Experiential Learning Theory. We argue that modern global business education must cultivate Symbiotic Cross-Border Intelligence—the integrated capacity to deploy, audit, and ethically govern intelligent systems across divergent sovereign, cultural, and regulatory jurisdictions. To operationalize this paradigm, the paper constructs an Adaptive Curriculum Co-Evolution Model paired with a Four-Tiered Experiential Learning Ecosystem that replaces passive lecturing with live cross-border algorithmic sandboxes, regulatory friction wargames, and multilingual stakeholder simulations. Drawing upon multi-semester pedagogical implementations across international finance, global supply chain resilience, and emerging-market entry courses, we demonstrate substantial improvements in students’ causal systems reasoning, hallucination forensics, and cross-cultural communicative agility. Finally, the paper addresses structural risks—including algorithmic monoculture, epistemic dependency, and extraterritorial data governance violations—and formulates an institutional compliance charter for business schools navigating the intelligent transformation of global commerce.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development

documents.abstract: У тезах досліджено можливості поєднання людиноцентричного підходу та технологій штучного інтелекту у системі управління відновленням українського бізнесу в умовах повномасштабної війни та повоєнної трансформації. Актуальність теми зумовлена масштабом руйнувань, дефіцитом трудових ресурсів, порушенням логістичних ланцюгів і необхідністю підвищення продуктивності підприємств. Мета дослідження — обґрунтувати концептуальну модель управління відновленням бізнесу, у якій штучний інтелект посилює управлінські можливості, а людина залишається центральним суб'єктом ухвалення рішень. Методологічну основу становлять аналіз і синтез наукових та аналітичних джерел, порівняння міжнародних рекомендацій, систематизація практик цифрової трансформації та концептуальне моделювання. У результаті визначено чотири взаємопов'язані компоненти запропонованої моделі: людиноцентричне лідерство й розвиток компетентностей; застосування ШІ для аналітики та підтримки рішень; адаптивна організація бізнес-процесів; відповідальне управління даними, ризиками й результатами. Обґрунтовано, що ефективність відновлення залежить не від самого факту впровадження технологій, а від їх узгодження з потребами працівників, клієнтів і громад, прозорості алгоритмічних рішень та збереження людського контролю. Практичне значення результатів полягає у можливості використання моделі малими й середніми підприємствами для підвищення стійкості, інноваційності та конкурентоспроможності.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to support intrusion detection and threat investigation. However, accurate predictions and explainable outputs do not necessarily lead to appropriate human reliance: analysts may over-rely on incorrect recommendations or unnecessarily reject reliable ones. This work proposes a human-centric trust-calibrated framework that integrates an AI-driven Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), online estimation of analyst trust and cognitive load, and adaptive explanation selection within a closed-loop security interface. The NIDS combines traffic and textual threat representations to provide threat predictions, calibrated reliability estimates, and semantic evidence. Behavioral and interaction signals are processed through a probabilistic state-space model to estimate the analyst state, while a reliability-aware controller dynamically adjusts explanation depth and evidence granularity according to the Trust-Calibration Error (TCE), which captures the mismatch between inferred analyst trust and current NIDS reliability. Rather than treating trust estimation or calibration as standalone objectives, we investigate whether their integration improves operational human–AI performance under varying NIDS reliability. A controlled SOC-oriented evaluation compares the proposed trust-calibrated policy with static and trust-agnostic adaptive explanation strategies in terms of analyst decision quality, inappropriate reliance, investigation efficiency, and cognitive workload. Empirical evaluation across 2160 trials with 36 participants demonstrates that the proposed trust-calibrated policy improves decision accuracy from 81.4% to 89.3%, corresponding to an increase of 7.9 percentage points, curtails Automation Bias Rate (ABR) from 43.1% to 22.2% (31/72 to 16/72, representing a 48.4% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 21.8%, a 49.4% reduction), and decreases Inappropriate Rejection Rate (IRR) from 18.8% to 11.0% (122/648 to 71/648, representing a 41.8% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 18.9% to 10.9%, a 42.3% reduction), while lowering trust miscalibration error from 0.184 to 0.101. Crucially, these reliance gains are accompanied by a reduction in subjective workload from 58.4 to 48.7 on the NASA-TLX scale and a decrease in mean investigation time from 30.2 s to 28.1 s. These findings indicate that effective human-centered security interfaces should not maximize trust or explanation richness, but dynamically promote reliance that is consistent with the actual competence of the AI system.

Introduction: Mass casualty incidents, whether of natural or human origin, result in a high number of fatalities, often under conditions that render visual identification impossible. In this context, forensic dentistry stands out as a primary method for human identification, in accordance with the INTERPOL Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) protocol. Objective: To analyze the importance of the main human identification techniques used in forensic dentistry during mass casualty incidents, as well as the challenges encountered in their application. Methodology: This is a literature review conducted by searching the SciELO, PubMed, LILACS, and Google Scholar databases, using descriptors such as "forensic dentistry," "human identification," "identification techniques," and "dental arch," covering publications from 2016 to 2026. Results: The 20 studies analyzed showed that the comparison of antemortem and postmortem records, imaging exams (CBCT, intraoral scanning), and the analysis of anatomical characteristics and prostheses are the most widely used resources. The quality of dental records proved to be the main limiting factor, with reports of documentation failures, absence of complete odontograms, and lack of standardization. Digital technologies and artificial intelligence showed promising results, but still require validation in real-world scenarios. Conclusion: Forensic dentistry is essential for human identification in mass disasters, especially due to the resistance of teeth and the possibility of comparison with previous records. However, the effectiveness of the method depends on the quality and standardization of dental records, integration among multidisciplinary teams, and scientific validation of new technologies.

Although coal-mine accident reports contain intertwined risk factors, co-occurrence alone cannot establish causal direction or quantify the risk of accident occurrence. The symmetry of statistical co-occurrence and the potential asymmetry of conditional relationships highlight the difficulty of determining meaningful directions between risk factors. This study aims to identify factors associated with severity in reported coal-mine accidents and examine their conditional dependencies. Based on a sample of 800 accident investigation reports collected from 2010 to 2025, this study integrated text mining and expert review to extract and standardize 55 risk factors. Subsequently, the Apriori algorithm was employed to mine candidate associations, and expert prior knowledge was introduced to establish directional constraints, forming the basis for constructing a Bayesian network. The analysis extracted 274 association rules and constructed a network topology comprising 57 nodes and 187 directed edges. The comprehensive assessment revealed that factors such as ventilation, roof management, safety education and training, employee safety awareness, and gas accumulation have particularly significant impacts on accident severity. This study not only provides a quantitative, structured analytical framework for deconstructing the causes of complex accidents but also offers a scientific basis for coal mining enterprises to transition their safety management from passive post-event response to proactive, targeted pre-event control. It holds significant practical value for optimizing the allocation of safety resources and enhancing the intrinsic safety level of coal mines.

The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the marketing landscape, providing scalable efficiencies in ad creation. However, the consumer side of AI integration remains underexplored. Drawing on algorithm aversion theory, this research extends the literature by examining how consumer characteristics moderate the persuasive impact of AI- and human-designed ads. Across a pretest and six large-scale experimental studies involving 6,579 consumer evaluations in Japan, this research finds that advertisements with undisclosed AI authorship often outperform human-designed advertisements in enhancing ad perceptions of creativity, credibility, clarity, and mental imagery (i.e., stimulating vivid consumer imagination) and, consequently, increasing purchase intentions. However, AI-generated ads are less effective among consumers with more generative AI experience, higher education, greater product category involvement, and lower interest in science. In these consumer segments, human-designed ads often have the advantage. These findings extend algorithm aversion theory by providing indirect evidence consistent with an implicit mechanism through which consumer characteristics trigger implicit algorithm detection (i.e., sensing algorithmic markers) and implicit algorithm aversion (i.e., subconscious devaluation of perceived artificiality) without requiring explicit disclosure of AI authorship. The findings inform marketing practice by emphasizing the importance of consumer segmentation.

This article examines the integration of artificial intelligence and digital educational technologies into English language teaching within the global educational ecosystem. It analyzes the development of the professional and technological competencies of 21st-century teachers, the potential of computational linguistics in language education, and the pedagogical and psychological aspects of hybrid and distance learning. In contemporary education, the use of artificial intelligence-based tools plays an important role in addressing learners’ individual needs, developing language skills, enhancing learning motivation, and organizing the educational process effectively. At the same time, the application of digital technologies should be combined with teachers’ methodological expertise, critical thinking, information literacy, and pedagogical responsibility. Based on a theoretical and analytical approach, the article explores the pedagogical opportunities of integrating artificial intelligence tools into English language lessons, identifies existing challenges, and provides practical recommendations.

This article examines how artificial intelligence and digital technologies can improve modern education. It discusses personalized learning, student engagement, teacher support, and key challenges, including digital inequality, data privacy, and ethical use.

This paper examines, from a theoretical and methodological perspective, the inclusive and sustainable educational opportunities offered by the use of an artificial intelligence assistant to develop the design competencies of students enrolled in Technological Education programmes in a digital learning environment. It analyses the informational and advisory functions of an AI chatbot in addressing students' individual information needs, supporting the use of vocationally oriented learning materials, and facilitating independent project-based activities. The paper also substantiates the didactic conditions for using an artificial intelligence assistant while preserving students' autonomy.

documents.abstract: The popularization of agents, models, and tools incorporating artificial intelligence is a phenomenon that has recently mobilized social and educational spheres due to new ethical and academic considerations, as well as the difficulties that arise when designing and evaluating learning experiences. The purpose of this study was to characterize the meaning and assess the scope of references to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in teacher training programs for secondary education in Uruguay, within the current curriculum (Plan 2023). The study focuses on STEM-related specialties. Through a content analysis of 156 curricular documents, the context of AI references was quantified and interpreted. The results show that these references are given a more instrumental than critical meaning. The presence of the Computer Science Teacher Training specialty is relevant, given that the interdisciplinary nature of the STEM approach can contribute to deepening critical thinking, transversality, and curricular flexibility for the pedagogical inclusion of these emerging technologies in teacher training.

Objective: To examine burnout rates among nursing professionals reported in publications from 2022 to 2026, considering measurement differences, associated factors, and implications for care. Methods: A descriptive narrative literature review based on scientific studies and reviews published within the defined period. Results: A 2023 meta-analysis estimated a global burnout prevalence of 30.0% (95% CI: 26.0–34.0%). A 2025 umbrella review reported a pooled prevalence of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for reduced personal accomplishment. A Brazilian study published in 2026 involving 3,594 nursing workers identified moderate exhaustion in 42.29% of participants; this indicator should not be interpreted as an overall syndrome prevalence. Conclusion: Burnout is a major occupational health concern, and heterogeneous measurement approaches require cautious interpretation and organizational prevention.

This paper examines the socioeconomic, demographic, digital, and labour-market factors associated with Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) adoption and the barriers that prevent its use. Using nationally representative data for Spain from the 2025 Survey on Equipment and Use of ICT in Households, we distinguish between private, work-related, and educational uses of GAI and analyse the heterogeneous reasons for non-adoption. To account for the selective observation of barriers among non-users, we estimate a multivariate sample-selection model with valid exclusion restrictions. The results reveal significant inequalities in both GAI adoption and non-adoption barriers. GAI adoption is positively associated with human capital, digital resources, and technology-intensive work environments. Moreover, non-adoption barriers vary substantially across population groups, with older, less educated, and female individuals facing primarily skill- and information-related constraints, while more educated and digitally connected individuals are more likely to question the relevance of these technologies. The findings suggest that the emerging GAI divide reflects both traditional forms of digital inequality and heterogeneous informational, capability-related, and attitudinal barriers. Policies aimed at promoting inclusive GAI adoption should therefore combine digital-skills development, awareness-raising initiatives, and measures to strengthen trust in AI technologies.

documents.abstract: Mathematics anxiety and motivation shape how senior high school students engage with mathematics, but their joint influence on achievement has received limited attention in Philippine public schools. Grounded in the Integrated Cognitive-Emotional Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this descriptive-correlational study examined the influence of mathematics anxiety and motivation level on the academic achievement of 109 Grade 11 and 12 students at General Santos City National High School in School Year 2025–2026. Anxiety was measured in four dimensions with an instrument adapted from the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale, motivation in three dimensions with items adapted from the Academic Motivation Scale (α = .78 to .85), and achievement through first- and second-quarter mathematics grades. Chi-square and Pearson correlation were applied. Anxiety was High in all dimensions, with emotional and cognitive anxiety highest (M = 3.23). Students’ motivation was predominantly extrinsic (M = 3.30, Very High), followed by intrinsic motivation (M = 3.23, High), with amotivation Fair (M = 2.28). Achievement was Satisfactory and improved from 83.45 to 84.20. Age, sex, grade level, strand, and family income were associated with anxiety and motivation, while sex, grade level, and strand were associated with achievement. Anxiety was negatively related to achievement (r = −.42, p = .001), and motivation was positively related to it (r = .38, p = .002). The results are consistent with a model in which anxiety drains cognitive resources during evaluation while motivation sustains effort. A school mental health plan focusing on regulation at the point of performance, autonomous motivation, and family engagement is proposed.

documents.abstract: Competency-based education and training (CBET) requires graduates to apply knowledge, perform occupational tasks, solve practical problems, and exercise professional judgement in authentic work environments. This narrative review examined the meaning and educational significance of practicum, the relationship between classroom learning and workplace competence, potential implementation barriers, relevant international experiences, and strategies for strengthening practicum in Tanzania’s livestock training system. The review synthesised literature and documentary information on workplace learning, agricultural and technical training, and apprenticeship approaches in Tanzania and selected countries. The findings distinguish theoretical instruction, institution-based practical training, field activities, and structured workplace practicum as complementary but non-equivalent learning experiences. Effective practicum requires clearly defined learning outcomes, authentic occupational tasks, supervised participation, constructive feedback, documented learning, and competency-based assessment. The synthesis identified potential implementation barriers, including inadequate financing, limited placement opportunities, unclear institutional and employer responsibilities, insufficient supervisor preparation, safety and safeguarding concerns, and weak assessment arrangements. International and Tanzanian apprenticeship examples highlighted transferable principles of employer engagement, shared training responsibilities, structured supervision, and quality assurance. However, available evidence does not establish the prevalence of these barriers or the adequacy of practicum across all Tanzanian livestock training institutions. The review proposes a coordinated framework integrating curriculum alignment, approved placement hosts, progressive competency development, student protection, sustainable financing, employer partnerships, and continuous monitoring. Tanzania should establish context-sensitive practicum standards, assess institutional readiness, strengthen collaboration between training institutions and livestock-sector employers, and pilot and evaluate implementation before wider adoption. National empirical research is also needed to establish baseline conditions and assess practicum quality and outcomes. Institutionalising structured practicum could strengthen the relevance of livestock education and support graduate preparedness for employment

This paper examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies into language teaching. It explores their role in developing vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, writing, and independent learning. The study adopts a literature review approach and uses the SAMR model to discuss technology integration in education. It also highlights challenges such as the reliability of AI-generated feedback, learners’ dependence on AI tools, and unequal access to digital resources. The paper emphasizes that effective technology integration requires clear learning objectives, teacher guidance, and meaningful communication. It concludes that AI and digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, teachers in language education.

This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies can be integrated into English for Specific Purposes (ESP) reading instruction using discipline-specific texts. The problem addressed is the mismatch between the linguistic and conceptual demands of authentic professional materials and learners’ varying levels of reading proficiency. A qualitative, literature-based methodological design was employed, combining thematic synthesis of established ESP and reading scholarship with instructional design analysis. The principal result is a three-stage framework linking pre-reading preparation, guided while-reading analysis and post-reading transfer to specific AI-supported teacher actions and observable learning evidence. A worked example demonstrates implementation with a professional text and identifies safeguards for accuracy, privacy and learner autonomy. The framework is a proposed pedagogical model, not an experimentally validated intervention. The article concludes that AI is most useful when it supports purposeful reading, disciplinary meaning-making and teacher-led formative assessment rather than replacing authentic engagement with texts.

Developing a new medicine can cost two to three billion US dollars over ten to 17 years, and roughly nine of ten compounds entering first-in-human testing never reach regulatory approval. Drug repurposing can reuse existing pharmacological and safety information, although a new indication may require additional toxicology, formulation, dose or pharmacokinetic studies. This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence, computational pharmacology, network and systems pharmacology, multi-omics and polypharmacology inform repurposing hypotheses. We distinguish disease-first, drug-first, phenotype-first and patient-stratification approaches and qualitatively assess the evidence supporting individual candidates. The methods covered include drug-target and drug-disease prediction, virtual screening, molecular dynamics, free-energy estimation, off-target and toxicity prediction, network analysis, and perturbation-signature integration. These methods contribute complementary information and can be applied iteratively rather than in a fixed sequence. Network proximity, signature reversal and observational associations nominate candidates; experimental target engagement, causal mechanism and clinical efficacy require distinct evidence. Positive and negative clinical examples illustrate this distinction, while preprints are identified separately from peer-reviewed studies. Integration remains constrained by dataset bias, incomplete interactomes, limited transferability and external validation, alongside exposure, experimental, funding and regulatory challenges. Computational integration is making repurposing increasingly hypothesis-driven, but prospective clinical validation remains limited. Its translational value depends on reliable predictions and independent, indication-specific experimental and clinical evaluation.

In the 21st century, soft skills such as communication, critical thinking, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence are essential for personal and professional development. Unlike academic knowledge, they enhance the practical impact of what a person knows. As artificial intelligence (AI) develops rapidly, integrating it into education, and specifically into soft skills development, may accelerate learning. However, few existing solutions bring these skills together in a single system. Many learners prioritize academic knowledge because soft skills are not formally assessed and do not lead to a diploma. As a result, these skills are often neglected, although employers increasingly expect them in both international and domestic settings. This article explores how soft skills development can be combined in a single AI-based system. The pilot study draws on a survey of some respondents. The analysis examines how respondents currently use AI to develop soft skills, which skills they consider the most important and the most difficult to develop, and whether attitudes differ by age or occupation.

Recognising the challenges that international students face in integrating the Portuguese Education System, NOVA University launched a semester-long Foundation Program in 2017. Within this program, we introduced the Ideas Club course in 2020 to promote students’ engagement and facilitate long-term academic success. This paper examines whether and how the course has helped these students overcome cultural barriers and adapt to the European context. European issues serve as a guiding framework to help non-European students interact and discuss in constructive ways, thereby grasping the complexities of European reality. The course adopts a dialogic pedagogical approach, promoting student-led discussions on diverse topics while encouraging consciousness, critical reflection, and the dismantling of some stereotypes. Literature in international foundation education highlights the importance of self-determination theory in fostering intrinsic motivation, which is essential for the desired engagement and academic success. We show in this paper how the Ideas Club contributes to fostering intrinsic motivation.

documents.abstract: The intelligent transformation of the chemical industry has reshaped petrochemical production workflows and altered occupational-health risk landscapes. This paper delineates four typical operating scenarios for intelligent chemical manufacturing and develops a four-tier hierarchical risk indicator system covering objectives, criteria, factors, and measurable indicators. A hybrid entropy-weighted Bayesian-network evaluation model is established, where entropy weights calibrate prior probabilities of root-node inputs while conditional-probability tables are retained to characterize risk-coupling behaviors. Model performance is validated via time-series partitioning, multi-model benchmark comparisons, and cross-validation using Monte-Carlo simulations. An entropy-weighted TOPSIS multi-criteria decision-making method is adopted to rank intervention-target priorities, and discrete time-series analysis quantifies outcomes from a six-month closed-loop intervention program. Results demonstrate that human-machine interaction, psychological, and managerial risks dominate occupational-health hazards within intelligent chemical-production contexts. Three highly sensitive critical drivers are identified: operating-instruction error rate, risk-monitoring gap duration, and information-overload frequency. Multi-criteria decision analysis further reveals that high-sensitivity risk factors do not inherently represent optimal intervention targets. The proposed model achieves 88.2% prediction accuracy on time-series test datasets, and statistically significant overall-risk reduction is observed post-intervention. This work offers theoretical support for risk identification, equipment retrofitting, and worker-health protection for smart petrochemical sites, facilitating the synergistic advancement of chemical-industry intelligent modernization, operational safety, and employee occupational-health outcomes.

documents.abstract: Attack surface management (ASM) is moving from periodic, tool-centric scanning towards continuous, intelligence-driven assessment. This survey reviews 31 curated sources (2021–2026) covering autonomous penetration testing, LLM-based security agents, multi-agent architectures, reinforcement-learning (RL) planners, security-tool orchestration, attack-path analysis, vulnerability validation, and evaluation benchmarks. Each source was coded against a common schema (AI technique, agent architecture, event-driven support, adaptive tool selection, fallback, validation, attack-chain coverage, testbed, metrics, findings, limitations). We present a literature matrix, comparative tables, a taxonomy, and a gap analysis. Within the reviewed corpus, the literature is strong on agent reasoning and planning but documents few complete implementations of event-driven orchestration, quality-aware tool fallback, and systematic false-positive-reducing validation within a single evaluated framework. Evaluation is also fragmented across simulations, CTF-style benchmarks, and small vulnerable testbeds. FoundFirst AI, the authors’ AI-powered ASM project, is used only as practical motivation. This survey reports no new experimental results. Keywords—attack surface management, penetration testing, large language models, multi-agent systems, security orchestration, vulnerability validation, reinforcement learning, event-driven architecture.

Background: Interactive multimedia and educational games offer opportunities for elementary learning, but their mechanisms and outcome measures are heterogeneous.Aims: To synthesize the design features of interactive multimedia game-based learning (MMI-GBL), the evidence on student engagement, the implications for problem solving, and the methodological limitations of the field.Methods: This systematic literature review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting principles with descriptive mapping and narrative synthesis. A previously compiled 41-reference bibliography was reconciled into a retrospectively defined core set of 17 publications (2022–2026) and 24 supporting references. Core sources comprise seven empirical studies and ten secondary syntheses. Data were entered into a structured extraction matrix and appraised qualitatively by context and outcome construct.Results: Five empirical publications concern elementary or early elementary learners, including one complementary multimedia study, and address mathematics learning, task solving, computing terminology, and engagement. Recurring design features include coherent multimedia representations, explicit goals and missions, adaptive scaffolding, specific feedback, and opportunities to retry and reflect. Designs in which scaffolding and feedback prompted learners to choose strategies, explain, and revise were associated with learning and engagement gains, whereas rewards detached from reasoning contributed little. Behavioral and cognitive engagement were the dimensions most often evidenced; emotional and agentic engagement were rarely measured. Perceived usefulness or achievement does not directly measure problem-solving performance, and external meta-analytic estimates remain contextual.Conclusion: MMI-GBL is most effective when multimedia features, game mechanics, scaffolding, feedback, and teacher facilitation are aligned with meaningful learning activities. Further elementary-level research is needed to strengthen evidence on engagement and problem-solving outcomes.

This article analyzes the discursive functioning of questions in Instagram and Facebook posts, understood as a strategy for interpellating the interlocutor and generating engagement on social media. Grounded in Applied Linguistics, Discourse Analysis, and literacy studies, it draws on authors such as Benveniste, Bakhtin and Volochinov, Pêcheux, Orlandi, Kerbrat-Orecchioni, Maingueneau, Charaudeau, Paveau, Bucher and Helmond, Gerlitz and Helmond, Recuero, and Duffy and Chan, among others, to understand the question as an enunciative-discursive practice crossed by specific sociotechnical conditions. Adopting a qualitative, descriptive-interpretative approach, the study analyzes a corpus of twelve interrogative statements — six from Instagram and six from Facebook — collected between June and September of the current year through an exemplary, rather than statistical, sampling. The analysis shows that questions circulating on these platforms tend to organize themselves between two poles: genuinely interpellative questions, which constitute the interlocutor as a subject called upon to take a stance amid a conflict of meaning, and predominantly market-oriented questions, which summon the interlocutor primarily as an engagement metric — most statements, however, combine both logics in varying proportions. The results also reveal relevant differences between platforms: on Instagram, shaped by reels and carousels, the question tends to operate as a device for rapid identification and retention; on Facebook, sustained by a more extensive commenting culture and by sharing across timelines and groups, it favors personal narrative and a sense of co-authorship. The study concludes that the digital question constitutes a technodiscursive practice whose effectiveness stems from the articulation between language, interface, algorithms, and social participation, with relevant implications for critical literacy and for the teaching of Portuguese Language.

Idiom interpretation requires cultural knowledge, context, and pragmatic understanding that cannot be inferred from literal word meanings alone. This challenge is particularly important for isiZulu, a richly inflected Nguni Bantu language with limited representation in the web-scale corpora used to train modern large language models (LLMs). We compare three approaches to isiZulu idiom interpretation (zero-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with glossary evidence, and supervised fine-tuning on a purpose-built, context-rich corpus) across five open-weight LLMs, evaluating them on 323 held-out idioms. Performance is evaluated using automated metrics and human assessment by expert isiZulu speakers. Supervised fine-tuning provides the strongest overall improvement, increasing the mean human evaluation score from 2.61 to 3.68 out of 5. RAG also improves interpretation quality, although its gains are smaller and are not fully captured by conventional surface-level metrics. Across the fifteen model--condition systems, COMET aligns best with human assessment, whereas embedding cosine similarity is the only metric that does not align positively with it, suggesting that this metric should be validated against human judgement before being used to evaluate idiomatic interpretation in low-resource languages. We contribute the isiZulu Idiom Dataset, a morphology-aware retrieval pipeline, and a reusable protocol for evaluating LLM-based idiom interpretation in low-resource African languages.

documents.abstract: This paper presents IRIS, an Intelligent Real-Time Informa-tion System: a voice-first Android assistant designed to give visually impaired people real-time awareness of their surroundings. Visually impaired people mostly rely on white canes, Braille and screen readers, which detect only nearby obstacles or work only with prepared con-tent, while existing smart-glasses and single-purpose applications are expensive, hardware-dependent and scattered across many tools. To address this issue, the proposed system combines scene description, text reading, currency identification, recognition of familiar faces, ob-stacle alerts, spoken navigation and SOS alerts in a single smartphone application. A four-layer architecture, consisting of a user interface layer, an application logic layer, a core modules layer and a hardware layer, runs the core artificial intelligence on the device, with a command router linking the speech, vision, emergency and navigation services. Audio and haptic feedback make the system hands-free and real-time, while an SOS command sends an SMS with the live location and calls a caretaker. The system is therefore low-cost, accessible and runs on an ordinary smartphone. This paper presents the literature survey, problem identification, proposed system, system requirements and system design of IRIS

documents.abstract: This discussion paper considers selected questions that arise when juridical processes concern heterogeneous subjects and systems whose histories, dynamics, manifestations, and institutional positions differ. Causal and informational coupling can coexist with distinct interpretive frameworks: culturally differentiated human communities, human–AI arrangements, and human relationships with terrestrial animals and ecosystems can be interdependent while possessing different capacities, temporal scales, and evidentiary categories. The paper revisits seven interacting concerns examined in an earlier study of nonlinear juridical processes: critical transitions, historical dependence, distributed causation, partial observability, situated interpretation, reflexive intervention, and irreversibility. It asks how heterogeneity may modify their significance for particular juridical functions. A further question concerns the recognition of juridically relevant subjects, considered through distinct inquiries into moral consideration, legal personality, standing, representation, and responsibility. The paper develops a provisional comparative vocabulary and considers four settings: culturally differentiated human communities, human–AI administrative processes, terrestrial interspecies relations, and a hypothetical first-contact case. Existing legal materials, including selected human-rights, environmental, animal-welfare, and AI-governance instruments, provide selected illustrations for the comparative inquiry. Two schematic equations and six figures illustrate stipulated mechanisms. Empirical testing of juridical outcomes remains a separate research task. The paper aims to clarify distinctions that might help frame future doctrinal and empirical investigations. The inquiry remains focused on comparative questions of subject recognition, interpretive accessibility, and juridical justification.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for empiric antibiotic decision support, but it remains unclear whether contemporary systems behave similarly under the same clinical and stewardship constraints. We compared four LLM configurations on real internal medicine admissions using a common, auditable stewardship benchmark. Methods: This single-center, retrospective, paired, non-interventional shadow-mode study included 486 admissions from a previously published 493-admission internal medicine cohort. For each admission, the clinician-prescribed empiric regimen was compared with recommendations from OpenAI GPT-5.5, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Mistral Large 2512; OpenAI GPT-5.2 was analyzed separately as a supplementary legacy bridge. All LLMs received identical clinical content, local epidemiology context, antibiotic ontology, and three-field output schema. The primary endpoint was any contextually unsupported broad-spectrum escalation, defined by the study’s prespecified guardrail rules; the key secondary endpoint was a weighted contextual escalation penalty. Results: Clinician regimens met the primary endpoint in 16.7% of admissions. Rates were 13.0% for GPT-5.5 (paired risk difference [RD] −3.7 percentage points; Holm-adjusted p = 0.216), 15.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro (RD −1.6; Holm-adjusted p = 0.509), 29.8% for Claude Opus 4.7 (RD +13.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), and 31.9% for Mistral Large 2512 (RD +15.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Mean weighted contextual escalation penalty was 0.288 for clinician prescribing, 0.173 for GPT-5.5, 0.165 for Gemini, 0.510 for Claude, and 0.348 for Mistral. Global heterogeneity across contemporary LLMs was significant for both endpoints (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Contemporary LLM configurations were not interchangeable under the same stewardship benchmark. The benchmark measures stewardship-process performance (contextually unsupported escalation), not microbiological adequacy or missed coverage; fewer violations should therefore not be read as better overall therapy. These findings support configuration-specific, version-locked local evaluation before prospective shadow-mode and human-in-the-loop assessment.

documents.abstract: Troubleshooting in operational environments relies on expert knowledge that is often undocumented and highly contextual. Informal data sources, such as communication logs, may hold some of this information, but their unstructured nature makes interpretation challenging. In a preliminary case study with a telescope operations facility, we explored whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct troubleshooting strategies from chat logs. LLM outputs were compared against those produced by a novice human analyst by two expert evaluators. We also compared an LLM with additional technical information in the context window and LLM outputs augmented by another novice analyst. While the domain experts varied in their scoring, overall LLM-generated analyses were judged as higher quality and more accurate than human-produced outputs. Neither additional technical context nor human augmentation resulted in meaningful improvements. These preliminary findings suggest LLMs show promise for expert knowledge extraction and decision-support in operational environments.

Mutation testing is a powerful technique for ensuring software quality. However, the presence of equivalent mutants introduces unnecessary costs and biases, limiting its practical effectiveness. Although numerous equivalent mutant detection (EMD) methods have been proposed, they often face distinct challenges: pure-code analysis methods can be limited by their reliance on specific compiler infrastructures, while existing machine-learning approaches remain constrained by scarce training data and limited generalization to unseen mutants. Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse code-related tasks by better capturing program semantics. Yet their potential for EMD remains largely unexplored, particularly in the multi-lingual context. This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study on LLMs for EMD, using 3,302 Java and 1,088 C mutant pairs to benchmark against state-of-the-art methods, explore strategy variations, assess efficiency, and evaluate cross-lingual generalization. Experimental results show that LLM-based approaches achieve higher F1-scores than the evaluated traditional methods, with fine-tuned code embedding yielding the highest detection accuracy among the tested strategies. Moreover, LLM-based approaches strike a practical balance between effectiveness and efficiency with inference times comparable to existing machine-learning models. Importantly, fine-tuned LLMs demonstrate measurable generalization across programming languages. These findings establish LLMs as a viable and efficient approach for tackling the longstanding challenge of equivalent mutant detection, offering new directions for advancing mutation testing in practice.

Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

As a cutting-edge non-viral delivery system, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are revolutionizing the treatment of drugs and nucleic acids. LNPs are now recognized as adaptable, clinically validated nanocarriers due to their clinical success, as evidenced by approved siRNA therapies and extensively used mRNA vaccines. In order to facilitate effective intracellular cargo release, modern LNPs employ ionizable lipids, which are neutral under physiological conditions but become positively charged in acidic endosomes. Stability, encapsulation efficiency, biodistribution, and therapeutic efficacy have all been enhanced by developments in lipid chemistry, microfluidic manufacturing, surface engineering, and artificial intelligence-assisted formulation. However, obstacles to wider use still include low tissue specificity, ineffective endosomal escape, immunogenicity, production difficulties, and long-term safety. The evolution, composition, formulation, delivery methods, therapeutic uses, clinical translation, regulatory issues, and upcoming tactics like organ-selective targeting and CRISPR-Cas gene editing are all covered in this review.

Liquid biopsy offers repeated, minimally invasive molecular profiling of cancer, but its clinical value depends on the analyte, analytical platform, and intended use. In this Review, we evaluate current liquid-biopsy technologies for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment guidance, with a particular emphasize on tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (TDEVs) as a bridge between biomarker detection and therapeutic intervention. We examine genomic and epigenomic profiling, single-cell and single-vesicle analysis, and multi-omics integration as complementary approaches for assessing tumour burden, heterogeneity and treatment response. Circulating tumor DNA genotyping guides targeted therapy in selected advanced cancers, whereas many early-detection and vesicle-based applications require prospective validation. We highlight how the TDEV lipid bilayer protects diverse molecular cargo that reflects evolving tumour phenotypes and how TDEV-mediated communication contributes to metastasis, immune evasion and therapeutic resistance, creating opportunities to target pathogenic vesicle signalling. We also assess engineered vesicles from malignant and non-malignant cells as drug-delivery and cancer-vaccination platforms, while noting that tumour-derived carriers may retain oncogenic or immunosuppressive cargo. Most candidate vesicle biomarkers remain supported by retrospective studies, and therapeutic platforms are largely preclinical or in early clinical testing. We discuss the requirements for clinical translation, including reliable identification of tumour-derived vesicles, standardized workflows and prospective multicentre validation for diagnostics, and reproducible manufacturing, cargo characterization, potency testing and product-specific pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation for therapeutics. Finally, we consider how multimodal profiling and artificial intelligence might improve signal integration, and argue that clinical adoption will depend on demonstrating that vesicle-guided decisions and interventions improve patient outcomes.

The field of Library and Information Science (LIS) has faced identity challenges during periods of rapid technological innovation that alter established practices (Chu, 2010; Marcum, 2005). The rise of artificial intelligence, increasing emphasis on data and technology, and discussions of iSchool mergers raise fundamental questions about disciplinary identity, values, and relevance (Gioia & Thomas, 1996; Marques et al., 2024). As an interdisciplinary field, LIS has struggled to define itself within a single conceptual framework and has navigated the tensions between professional education and research (Audunson et al., 2007). These developments compel LIS educators and researchers to redefine knowledge production, management, and dissemination within the field.Building on prior work (Gibson et al., 2025; LIS Forward, 2023; 2025), this study examines how LIS epistemological core is represented and communicated as foundational knowledge in 40 LIS core course syllabi from 10 selected iSchools in the United States. Informed by Erduran and Kaya's (2019) definition of the “epistemic core,” this study employs collaborative thematic analysis to examine course titles, descriptions, learning objectives, and required materials. Based on the analysis, syllabi were coded into four categories: general research, special topics, professional skills development, and research methods. AI use disclaimers and guidance were also examined for any potential patterns across the syllabi. Core courses in MLIS (and related degrees) introduce emerging scholars and practitioners to what is considered foundational to the LIS field, potentially shaping their understanding of LIS epistemological core. The study findings contribute to ongoing efforts to clarify LIS identity, help shape future curricula, and articulate the field’s contributions to broader academic domains amid institutional mergers and shifting disciplinary boundaries in higher education.

Large language model (LLM) systems deployed in production are subject to a form of degradation that classical software is not: their behavior can change without a corresponding code change, because the underlying model, its provider-side weights, or the prompt scaffolding around it can shift independently of the application's own release cycle. Traditional regression testing, built around deterministic assertions, is poorly suited to this setting, because LLM outputs are open-ended, stochastic, and evaluated along dimensions –– tone, faithfulness, safety, format compliance –– that resist exact-match comparison. This paper presents LLM Maintainer, an open-source tool that treats a second LLM call as a judge, scoring a fixed suite of "golden prompts" against natural-language rubrics on every run, persisting the results, and flagging statistically meaningful drops relative to a rolling per-test-case baseline. We describe the system's architecture –– a YAML-configured test suite, an execution runner, a structured LLM-as-judge module, a regression-detection algorithm, a SQLite persistence layer, and a Flask dashboard –– and its command-line and dashboard-triggered workflows for both ad hoc and scheduled (cron-style) use. Because this work was produced in a network-restricted sandbox without access to the live Anthropic API, we report a fully disclosed, seeded, synthetic case study rather than presenting simulated data as genuine field results: we ran the actual, unmodified runner, judge, regression-detection, and persistence code for 30 simulated daily evaluation cycles (180 evaluated prompt-response pairs) against a six-case suite modeling a retail-banking customer-support assistant, with three deliberately injected incidents –– a transient API failure, a silent quality regression introduced by a system-prompt refactor, and a one-off output-format violation. The tool's naive, fixed-threshold rolling-baseline detector recovered five of six injected anomalies (83.3% recall) but also raised 18 flags attributable to ordinary sampling variance in a five-point ordinal judge scale (21.7% precision, F1 = 0.345), a quantitative finding that motivates statistically smoothed alternatives. We situate this design relative to LLM-as-a-judge evaluation research, holistic benchmarking, documented behavioral drift in commercial LLMs, and concept-drift detection in classical machine learning operations, and we discuss the threats to validity inherent in judge-based scoring –– including self-preference and verbosity bias –– alongside concrete mitigations. We conclude that continuous, judge-in-the-loop regression testing is a necessary complement to pre-deployment benchmarking for maintaining LLM-integrated software, while cautioning that naive thresholding requires the same statistical care long established in the concept-drift literature.

Locating and fixing software faults is challenging. Traditional Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) uses test coverage and failure data but often suffers from low accuracy due to a lack of semantic understanding of code. Deep-learning approaches can improve localization, but require extensive training data and computational resources. Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative with stronger code reasoning capabilities. However, existing LLM-based fault localization techniques still struggle at the repository level due to large context windows and positional bias, in which important debugging signals may be buried in large contexts. In this work, we introduce LLM4FL , a multi-LLM-agent-based fault localization technique designed to address these challenges. LLM4FL uses three specialized agents. The Context Extraction Agent divides and prioritizes covered methods into token-fitting groups using an order-aware strategy based on Ochiai suspiciousness scores. The Debugger Agent navigates the repository through graph-based retrieval to generate failure reasoning and rank suspicious methods. The Reviewer Agent then re-evaluates and re-ranks the results through iterative self-refinement and verbal reasoning. Evaluated on Defects4J, LLM4FL improves Top-1 accuracy over prior LLM-based approaches, including AutoFL and SoapFL , by 14.5% and 4.58%, respectively. Our ablation study further highlights the importance of LLM4FL's design choices, with failure reason generation improving Top-1 performance by 12.5% and order-aware division substantially improving localization accuracy by 18.07%.

Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) are transforming the way modern medicine is practiced, with more accurate disease detection, clinical decision making, personalized medicine, and public health surveillance. This paper reviews their applications in clinical medicine, epidemiological surveillance, digital health technologies and population health care. It also includes cyber security threats like privacy issues, enemy attacks, and data breaches, ransom ware.
